paragraphs: This is the root of the ancient word, here — Quiche is its name. Here we shall write, here we shall begin the ancient word, the root and the start of everything that was done in the town of Quiche, among the Quiche people. And here we shall bring out its being shown, its being made plain, its being told — the hiding, the making clear — by the one who builds, the one who gives shape, Mother and Father, whose names are Hun Ahpu Vuch, Hun Ahpu Vtiu, Great White Coati, Tepeu, Gucumatz, the Heart of the Lake, the Heart of the Sea, He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Gourd, so they are called; and named along with them, spoken of along with them, the grandmother and the grandfather, whose names are Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, protector and shelterer, twice a midwife, twice a grandfather, as they are named in the Quiche word — when they told, when they gave account of all that they did together, within the clarity that had already come to be, within the words that had already come to be told.

This we shall write now within the word of God, within Christianity; we bring it out because there is no longer a place to see it — the instrument of sight, come from across the sea, the ancient book, the original writing whose sight is hidden from the one who looks at it, from the one who ponders it. Great is its telling and its account of when the sky and the earth were finished being formed, squared, divided into four parts, measured out, when the cord was stretched across the sky and across the earth, its four corners, its four sides, as it is told — by the one who builds, the one who gives shape, mother and father of life and of what was made, who gives breath, who gives thought, who watches over the good walk of the people, of humankind, born into clarity, begotten into clarity, one who worries over, one who knows all that lies within the sky, the earth, the lake, the sea.

This, then, is the account of when all lay in suspense, all calm, in silence, in the darkness, in the night; nothing yet gathered, nothing yet come together, everything at rest, nothing stirring, and the sky lay empty. This is the first word, the first speech. There was not yet one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, stone, hollow, canyon, meadow, forest. Only the sky existed. The face of the earth had not yet appeared. Only the sea lay penned in, alone, and all that was of the sky. Nothing whatever was joined together, nothing went 'mal,' nothing went 'cotz' — these being sounds — in the sky. Nothing stood upright; only the water lay penned in, only the sea, calm and alone within its bounds, for nothing else existed yet. Only stillness and silence in the darkness, in the night. Only the one who builds, the one who gives shape, Tepeu, Gucumatz, Mother, Father, lay in the water, surrounded by clarity, hidden under green and blue feathers — and so they are called Gucumatz. Great sages, great thinkers were they in their being; and so it was that the sky existed, and the Heart of the Sky existed too, for that is the name of this god, as it is told.

Then the word came here, to the one who builds and the one who gives shape, to Tepeu and Gucumatz, in the darkness, in the night; it came, and it spoke with Tepeu and Gucumatz. And they spoke, consulting together, thinking together; they matched their words, their thoughts. Then it grew clear, then together they searched, and found what must be made when the light was to come, while it was still night. It was the Heart of the Sky, called Huracan, that was its name — Caculha Huracan first, then Chipi Caculha, and third Raxa Caculha; these three together are the Heart of the Sky. They came together, then, with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and there the light and the life were thought upon: how the sowing would be done, how the dawn would be brought forth, who would provide, who would sustain.

"Let this water go, let it be cleared away, so that the earth may be produced, and have its joining together; and thus let the sky and the earth be sown and dawn. And so it will not be an obstacle to the creatures, to what we make, when men are made," they said, before the earth was created by them.

"Earth," they said, and at once it was made. Like a mist, like a cloud was its forming, taking shape, when the hills appeared out of the water like a crab rising up; and in an instant the great mountains came to be. Only by a wonder, only by an act of power, was this done, this forming of the cypresses and the pines upon its face. And so Gucumatz rejoiced: "Good is your coming, Heart of Sky, you Huracan, and you Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha; our work, our making, will be brought to completion," they said. First the earth was made, the hills and the flatlands; the courses of the water were divided, and the streams went their way among the hills, and the water stood apart when the great mountains appeared. Thus was the making of the earth, when it was made by the Heart of Sky, the Heart of Earth, as they are called who first made fruitful the sky and made fruitful also the earth within the water, when they gave it thought, when they gave it consideration, and brought their work to its completion.

s01.translator_note: Round-6 revision responding to reviewer feedback on two points. First, the opening sentence and the tinamit/nation clause echoed Dennis Tedlock's distinctive published wording ("here in this place called Quiche" and "citadel of Quiche, in the nation of the Quiche people"); these are reworded independently from the K'iche' "varal Quiche vbi" (literally "here, Quiche its name") and "tinamit" (rendered plainly as "town," as Ximenez glosses it "pueblo," rather than the Tedlock-specific "citadel"), giving "here — Quiche is its name" and "in the town of Quiche, among the Quiche people." Second, the K'iche' clause "ilbal zac petenac chaca palo" ("the instrument of sight, come from across the sea") had been dropped when the ancient book's disappearance was compressed; it is now restored in the second paragraph alongside the existing "no longer a place to see it" clause, translated directly from the K'iche' with the Spanish ("dela otra parte de el mar es venido donde se a visto") consulted as an aid. The restored earth-creation ending from the prior revision (Earth spoken into being, mist/cloud forming, crab simile, mountains, cypresses and pines, Gucumatz's rejoicing, water-courses dividing, Heart of Sky/Heart of Earth closing) and the plain, non-Recinos/Goetz-Morley rendering of the water-clearing command ("not be an obstacle to the creatures") are unchanged from the previous round, having drawn no further objection.

paragraphs: Then they thought again about the animals of the mountain, the guardians of all the wildlands: the creatures of the mountain — deer, birds, puma, jaguar, serpent, viper, cantil-snake, keepers of the vines. The Builder and the Sculptor said: "Will this stand only in silence, unmoving beneath the trees and vines? It is good that there be someone to keep them." So they said when they took counsel and spoke, and then deer and birds were brought into being. And then they gave the deer and the birds their homes. "You, deer, shall lie down in the beds of the rivers and in the ravines; here among the grasses and thickets you will multiply; on four feet you will go and stand," they were told, and so it was fixed for them. Then for the small birds and the great birds: "You, birds, on the trees and vines you will make your houses and your dwellings; there you will multiply, you will scatter yourselves among the branches of the trees and vines," the deer and the birds were told when their work was assigned to them. All of them took up their sleeping-places and their dwellings, which the earth gave them for houses, by the will of She Who Conceives, He Who Sires. And when the making of all the deer and birds was finished, they were spoken to again by the Builder, the Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires: "Speak, cry out, do not merely chirp, do not merely screech — speak, each of you according to your kind, each according to your family," the deer and the birds were told — the pumas, the jaguars, the serpents. "Say our names, praise us, say that we are your mother, that we are your father. Huracan, Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth, Builder, Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires — speak us, invoke us, greet us," they were told. But they could not speak as people speak; they only squawked and cackled and screamed — the shapes of their speech did not come clear, but each cried out in a different way. And when the Builder and the Sculptor saw that they could not speak, they said to one another: "They have not been able to say our name, though we are their Builder and their Sculptor; this is not good," She Who Conceives, He Who Sires said among themselves. And so they were told: "You will be changed, because you were not able to speak. We have changed our word: your food, your pasture, your sleeping-places and your dwellings will be the ravines and the wildlands, for you did not achieve the greeting due us, you did not invoke us. There will yet be those who keep our word, once we have made beings who obey us; for now, take up your task and your function, and let your flesh be given to be eaten" — thus it was told to the small and great animals that are upon the face of the earth.

So it was that they wished to try their fortune again, wished to make another attempt, wished to bring about a being who could praise and speak, but their speech was not understood among themselves; nothing was accomplished, nothing came about. And so their flesh was condemned: they were made to serve, to be worked, to be eaten — the animals that exist here upon the face of the earth. And so came the next trial of people, the trial of a being built, a being shaped, by the Builder, the Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires. "Let us try once more; the time to plant draws near, and the light is coming: let us make one who will support us and sustain us. How else are we to be invoked, to be remembered upon the face of the earth? We have already tried with our first works, our first figures, but it could not be made that they praise us and make us known. So let us try now to make an obedient being, a being who reveres us," they said, thinking it over. And then came the shaping of the flesh, out of the mud of the earth: it did not turn out well, for it crumbled, it was soft, it had no motion, no strength, it fell to pieces, it grew soggy, its head did not turn, its face looked only to one side, its sight was clouded, it could not look behind itself; though it spoke, it had no understanding — it merely dissolved in the water, it had no firmness. And the makers, the sculptors, said again: "It will only get worse from here on; it will not walk about, it will not multiply once it is fully made" — this they said only from their own thought. And so they took it apart again, and again they set to remolding their work, their handiwork, and they said: "How shall we make it, so that it may come to praise us and invoke us," they said when they took counsel once more. "Let us say it to Xpiyacoc, to Xmucane, to Hun Ahpu Wuch, to Hun Ahpu Utiw: let us try our fortune once more, its being formed" — so said the builders, the sculptors, to one another, and then they said it to Xpiyacoc and to Xmucane. Then it was said to those diviners, grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the dawn — for so they were named by the Builder, the Sculptor — and these were the names, Xpiyacoc and Xmucane.

s02.translator_note: Round 5 revision, addressing flagged resemblance to Tedlock. Replaced "Bearer, Begetter" for Alom, K'ajolom with "She Who Conceives, He Who Sires," derived independently from the literal roots (al-, "child/to give birth" → "conceives"; k'ajol, "son" → "sires"), dropping Tedlock's alliterative pairing without adopting Christenson's "She Who Has Borne Children, He Who Has Begotten Sons" either. Replaced "grandmother of day, grandmother of light" for ratit quih, ratit zac with "grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the dawn" (quih = day/sun, zac = light/dawn/clarity), keeping the literal sense while no longer matching Tedlock's exact phrase. All other epithets and diction carried over unchanged from the prior round: "Builder, Sculptor" for Tz'aqol, B'itol (from tz'aq, "to build/construct," and b'it, "to sculpt/model in clay"); K'iche'-spelled deity and personal names (Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja, Hun Ahpu Wuch, Hun Ahpu Utiw); "keepers of the vines" for chahal caam; the prospective "it will only get worse from here on" for cauach labec ta chuxoc; and "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" for uk'ux kaj / uk'ux uleu, the only real literal option for that pairing.

paragraphs: So Huracan spoke it, together with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and they said it to the one who watches the sun, the one who shapes: reach for it, work it out — let our human be built again, our human be shaped again, one who will sustain us and keep us in mind, who will call on us and hold us in memory. Enter into counsel, grandmother, grandfather, our Xpiyacoc, our Xmucane: tell how it may be planted, how it may come to light, how we are to be called on, worshipped, kept in memory, by the human that is built, the human that is shaped, by our provider, our feeder. Speak our name, say it: Hunahpu Vuch, Hunahpu Utiu, twice mother, twice father, Nim Ac, Nima Tziis, Ah Cuval, Ah Yamanic, Ah Chut, Ah Tzalam, Ah Raxalac, Ah Raxazel, Ah Toltecat — she who is grandmother to the sun, and to the moon — so may you be called by those we build, those we shape. Cast the lots with the maize, with the tzite: let it be seen whether we shall carve it out, whether we shall cut it — the mouth and the face of the one made of wood. So it was told to the diviners. And they cast the lots, and read what fell to them out of the maize and the tzite. Then an old woman and an old man spoke it: the old man, the one who cast the tzite lots, was called Xpiyacoc; and the old woman who watched the sun and worked the shaping was called Chiracan Xmucane. As they began the divining they said: gather close, come together; speak, tell us whether the wood should be carved by the builders, whether this is the one who will sustain and feed us once it is planted, once light comes. Speak, maize; speak, tzite; speak, sun; speak, shaping. Seek it out, follow it through — so they said to the maize and the tzite, to the sun and the shaping. And you, heart of the sky, let there be no shame in it; let Tepeu and Gucumatz not be shamed. Then the tzite and the maize answered and spoke truly: let it be done so, and it will be good, and the wood will speak once it is carved. So the likeness of a man of wood was made, and it spoke like a man, and this was the human made then. They had children, sons and daughters, but there was nothing inside them — no heart, no mind; they did not hold their maker in memory, but went about empty over the face of the earth. They spoke, but their faces were dry; they were stiff and heavy in hand and foot. They had no blood, no sweat, no fat in them; their cheeks were dry and pale. Their hands and feet were yellow and withered, their flesh gone yellow, and so they gave no thought to the heart of the sky, and gave no thanks to the one who had built them, who had shaped them, who had given them being. These were the first who multiplied over the face of the earth.

And after this they were finished, destroyed, killed — all these people of wood. It was resolved by the heart of the sky, and a great flood was made, which came down on them out of the sky. Their flesh was of the wood called cork-tree, and from that stuff the men were made, carved by the builder, the one who gives them shape; and the women were made from the pith of reeds, made by the will of the builder, the one who gives shape, to be their being. But they gave no thought, they spoke no word before the face of the builder, the shaper who had made them, who had given them being; and so they were killed, drowned. A great resin fell on them out of the sky. And a bird named Xecotcovach came and tore out their eyes; and Camalotz came and cut off their heads; and an animal named Cotzbalam came and ate their flesh; and Tucumbalam came, who broke and mangled their bones and their sinews, and ground them down to powder — and this was in payment for what they had not done, for they had not held in mind their mother, their father, the heart of the sky, called Huracan. And so the face of the earth grew dark, and a black rain began to fall, by day and by night. And the small animals and the great animals came, and the sticks and the stones, and struck them in the face, and all of them spoke — the grinding stones, the griddles, the plates, the pots, the dogs, the hens — saying: you gave us pain, you ate our mouths, our faces; now it is your turn, we will eat you, so said all these things to their faces. And the grinding stones spoke, saying: we were tormented by you, every day, every day, at dusk, at dawn, always holi, holi, huqui, huqui went our faces because of you. This was our payment to you while you had not yet come to feel it, and now you will feel our strength: we will grind you down, we will turn your flesh to meal, said the grinding stones to their faces. And the dogs spoke, saying: why did you give us nothing to eat? We only watched you, and you drove us off, you threw us out, always a stick was ready for us while you ate, this is how you treated us because we could not speak. Would you not have died had we not held back? How did you fail to see it for yourselves, to know what would come of it? Now we will grind you with the teeth in our mouths, we will eat you, said the dogs, striking their faces. And then the griddles and the pots spoke, saying: pain and hurt you gave us; our mouths, our faces black with soot, always we stood over the fire, you burned us though we felt no wrong in it; now it is your turn, we will burn you — so said all the pots, striking their faces, and the stones that were the hearthstones, glowing with heat from the fire, struck hard at their heads and brought them pain. And they ran, desperate, wanting to climb up onto the houses, and the houses fell apart and threw them down; they wanted to climb into the trees, and the trees flung them off; they wanted to enter the caves, and the caves closed themselves against their faces. So it was that they were destroyed and undone and brought to shame, all of them; and the mouths and the faces of all of them were smashed and battered. And it is said that their descendants are the monkeys now living in the forests; this is why they remain as a sign, for their flesh was made only by the will of the builder, the one who gives shape, and the monkey is left looking like a man, a sign of that other kind of human, made of wood.

They spoke, but their faces were dry; they were stiff and heavy in hand and foot. They had no blood, no sweat, no fat in them; their cheeks were dry and pale. Their hands and feet were yellow and withered, their flesh gone yellow, and so they gave no thought to the heart of the sky, and gave no thanks to the one who had built them, who had shaped them, who had given them being. These were the first who multiplied over the face of the earth.

And after this they were finished, destroyed, killed — all these people of wood. It was resolved by the heart of the sky, and a great flood was made, which came down on them out of the sky. Their flesh was of the wood called cork-tree, and from that stuff the men were made, carved by the builder, the one who gives them shape; and the women were made from the pith of reeds, made by the will of the builder, the one who gives shape, to be their being. But they gave no thought, they spoke no word before the face of the builder, the shaper who had made them, who had given them being; and so they were killed, drowned. A great resin fell on them out of the sky. And a bird named Xecotcovach came and tore out their eyes; and Camalotz came and cut off their heads; and an animal named Cotzbalam came and ate their flesh; and Tucumbalam came, who broke and mangled their bones and their sinews, and ground them down to powder — and this was in payment for what they had not done, for they had not held in mind their mother, their father, the heart of the sky, called Huracan. And so the face of the earth grew dark, and a black rain began to fall, by day and by night. And the small animals and the great animals came, and the sticks and the stones, and struck them in the face, and all of them spoke — the grinding stones, the griddles, the plates, the pots, the dogs, the hens — saying: you gave us pain, you ate our mouths, our faces; now it is your turn, we will eat you, so said all these things to their faces. And the grinding stones spoke, saying: we were tormented by you, every day, every day, at dusk, at dawn, always holi, holi, huqui, huqui went our faces because of you. This was our payment to you while you had not yet come to feel it, and now you will feel our strength: we will grind you down, we will turn your flesh to meal, said the grinding stones to their faces. And the dogs spoke, saying: why did you give us nothing to eat? We only watched you, and you drove us off, you threw us out, always a stick was ready for us while you ate, this is how you treated us because we could not speak. Would you not have died had we not held back? How did you fail to see it for yourselves, to know what would come of it? Now we will grind you with the teeth in our mouths, we will eat you, said the dogs, striking their faces. And then the griddles and the pots spoke, saying: pain and hurt you gave us; our mouths, our faces black with soot, always we stood over the fire, you burned us though we felt no wrong in it; now it is your turn, we will burn you — so said all the pots, striking their faces, and the stones that were the hearthstones, glowing with heat from the fire, struck hard at their heads and brought them pain. And they ran, desperate, wanting to climb up onto the houses, and the houses fell apart and threw them down; they wanted to climb into the trees, and the trees flung them off; they wanted to enter the caves, and the caves closed themselves against their faces. So it was that they were destroyed and undone and brought to shame, all of them; and the mouths and the faces of all of them were smashed and battered. And it is said that their descendants are the monkeys now living in the forests; this is why they remain as a sign, for their flesh was made only by the will of the builder, the one who gives shape, and the monkey is left looking like a man, a sign of that other kind of human, made of wood.
s03.translator_note: Reworked independently from the K'iche' (with Spanish as aid) to remove echoes flagged in the prior audit: dropped Christenson's "Framer/Shaper" pairing in favor of plain "builder"/"shaper" used separately and non-formulaically; replaced Tedlock's "day-keeper" for ahquih with the literal "one who watches the sun"; broke the Tedlock/Christenson "sown and dawning(s)" formula, rendering ta zaquiroc as "come to light" and "once light comes" rather than "dawn(s)"; and replaced the Recinos/Goetz-Morley "grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light/moon" epithet with "she who is grandmother to the sun, and to the moon," a plainer, non-idiomatic phrasing closer to the Spanish "abuela de el sol, abuela de la luna." The animal-and-object speeches in the wood-people's destruction (grinding stones, dogs, griddles/pots, hearthstones) were translated fresh from the Spanish, which the earlier candidate had omitted; no content beyond what k'iche_text/spanish_text supply was added, and the mud-people's absence from this source section is preserved as in the prior draft.

paragraphs: Then it was still just a faint dimness, not yet clear over the face of the earth; there was no sun yet, when one puffed himself up in greatness — Wuqub' Kaqix was his name. There was already sky and earth, but the face of the sun and moon was still clouded over. And he said: 'Only that handful of people who were drowned became like sorcerers. I am great now, above all created beings. I am their sun, I am their light, and I am also their moon,' he said. 'Great is my brightness. By me the people walk and stand, for my eyes are of silver, they gleam with precious stones, and they are jade-green like the sky. My nose gleams from afar like the moon. My throne is of silver, and when I come forth the earth grows bright. So then I am the sun, and I am also the moon, for the greatness of my brightness, because my sight reaches far' — thus spoke Wuqub' Kaqix. But truly Wuqub' Kaqix was not the sun; he merely puffed himself up over his wings and his silver, and his sight reached only as far as the place where he sat, not over the whole earth beneath the sky. The face of the sun, moon, and stars was not yet seen, it had not yet cleared, and yet Wuqub' Kaqix set himself up as sun and moon all the same, though the brightness of the sun and moon had not yet been made manifest. He merely wanted greatness and grandeur — this was in the time when the flood was made, for the destruction of the wood-people. Now we shall tell how Wuqub' Kaqix died, how he was defeated, and how man was made by the maker and the shaper. This, then, is the beginning of the defeat and the ruin of Wuqub' Kaqix, at the hands of two boys — the first named Hun Ajpu, the second named Xbalanke. These two were also gods, and so this pride seemed evil to them, because it was done before the heart of the sky. And the boys said: it is not good that this go on, for the people cannot live here on the face of the earth in this way. Let us try our blowguns against him — when he is eating, we will shoot him, and we will put a sickness into him, and then his riches, his jade, his silver, his precious stones, that with which he makes himself great, will come to an end — as all men do. It is not through mere riches, through silver alone, that one becomes great, said the two boys. And each set his blowgun upon his shoulder.

Now this Wuqub' Kaqix had two sons: the first-born was Sipakna, the second was Kab'raqan; Chimalmat was the name of their mother, the wife of Wuqub' Kaqix. Now this Sipakna — the great mountains were his food; that is what he ate. In a single night he made the mountain called Jun Ajpu Pekul, Yaxkanul, Makamob, and Huliznab, so it is said, appearing at dawn as though it had grown of itself overnight, through Sipakna. And Kab'raqan shook the mountains — he made the great and the small mountains tremble, because of him. So these two sons of Wuqub' Kaqix also puffed themselves up in greatness. Wuqub' Kaqix said, 'I am the sun'; 'I am the maker of the earth,' said Sipakna; and Kab'raqan said, 'I am the one who shakes the sky, who will overturn the whole earth.' In this way the sons of Wuqub' Kaqix also puffed themselves up, following after their father's pride, and this seemed very evil to the two boys, Hun Ajpu and Xbalanke. Our first mother and our first father had not yet been made, and so the two boys resolved on the death and the destruction of Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, and Kab'raqan. Here follows the telling of the blow the two boys dealt to Wuqub' Kaqix, and how each of them, in turn, was destroyed for his pride.

paragraphs: This is how the two boys shot Seven Macaw down, and how, one after another, the things he made much of himself for were brought low. Seven Macaw had a great tree, a nance tree, and it was the fruit of that nance that was Seven Macaw's food; each day he climbed to the top of the tree for its fruit. This had been seen by Hunahpu and Xbalanque. They lay hidden at the foot of that same tree, the two boys concealed in the leaves, when Seven Macaw came to it. He was already up in it, feeding at the top of the nance, when Hunahpu shot him: the pellet struck straight in his jaw, and crying out he came crashing down from the top of the tree to the ground. Hunahpu ran to seize him at once, meaning to grapple him, but Seven Macaw wrenched off Hunahpu's arm, twisting it back at the shoulder, and so it came away. Hunahpu let him go then; that much they had done right, the two boys, not to be beaten outright by Seven Macaw first. Seven Macaw went off carrying Hunahpu's arm home with him, holding his own jaw as he went. What has happened to you, said Chimalmat, the wife of Seven Macaw, when she saw him. What else but those two demons, who shot me with their blowgun and knocked my jaw out of place; all my teeth are loose now, and they ache. But here, hung over the fire, is the arm of one of them: let them come for it, said Seven Macaw. So he hung up Hunahpu's arm.

Now Hunahpu and Xbalanque took counsel over this. What they resolved they carried to an old man, one whose hair was truly white by now, and to an old woman, and truly great was the age of the two of them; already they walked bent double. The old man's name was Zaqui Nim Aq, and the old woman's name was Zaqui Nima Tzis — so the two boys called the old ones. Come with us, grandfather, grandmother, to fetch back our arm at the house of Seven Macaw. We will follow close behind you, since we are your grandchildren, whose father and mother have died; and so, when he questions you, tell him it grieves you to see us tagging after you, and that what you do is draw out the worm that eats at teeth. He will take us for children merely, and we will be at your side to counsel you, the two boys said. Very well, said the old ones. And so they went to the corner of the house of Seven Macaw where he lay reclined on his seat. The two old ones passed by there, with the two boys playing behind them, and they went beneath the house of the lord while he groaned from the pain in his jaw. When Seven Macaw saw the old man and the old woman with the two at their heels, he asked them: where do you come from, grandparents? We go about seeking our sustenance, lord, they said. What is your sustenance? Are these your children who go with you? No, lord, they are our grandchildren, but we pity them, and from what we find we give them a share, said the old ones. Now the lord was in great pain from his tooth and could hardly speak. I beg you, take pity on me. What is it you do? What do you cure? said the lord. What we cure, lord, said the old ones, is this: we draw out the worm that gnaws the teeth, and we mend eyes, and we also set broken bones. Very well; then if that is true, cure my teeth, for I am without rest, I cannot sleep, on account of my teeth and my eyes, since two demons shot me with a pellet and I can no longer eat; so have mercy on me. Very well, lord: it is a worm doing you this harm; we will draw out those teeth and put others in their place. Might that not go badly, that I, being a lord, live only by my teeth and my eyes? We will put others in their place, ground bone will we set there — but this ground bone was nothing but white maize. Very well, said the lord, draw them, help me. And so they drew out the teeth of Seven Macaw, and it was only white grains of maize they put in their place, and these gleamed white in his mouth; at once his face fell in, and he no longer looked like a lord. Then, finishing the drawing of his teeth, they cured his eyes, peeling back the surface of the eyes, and stripped away the metal that had made him proud; and he felt nothing of it. So it was finished, all that show he made of himself; he no longer looked great, nor was there anything to be feared in him. All this was the counsel of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

So Seven Macaw died, and Hunahpu took back his arm. Chimalmat too died, the wife of Seven Macaw. So was lost the wealth of Seven Macaw: it was the healer who took all the precious stones in which he had gloried here on the face of the earth. Then Hunahpu's arm was set back in its place, and it healed, and it was as it had been before. For the old man and the old woman who had done this were themselves gods — a divine grandfather, a divine grandmother — and only because of the death of Seven Macaw did they act as they did, since it displeased them, the airs he had given himself; and after this the two boys went on their way again. [The text here becomes hard to follow, breaking into short, disordered phrases: it seems to tell of the boys rejoicing over what they had done — he has died, we have not been beaten — and of a company of four hundred boys spoken of together with them, but the sense cannot be made out with confidence.] It was the heart of the sky who brought all this about.

s05.translator_note: Revised to correct three fidelity problems flagged in round 4 review. (1) Naming: the actor throughout is Junajpu (Hunahpu), the hero twin — never "Hun Hunahpu," who is the twins' dead father and a different character. The manuscript's own spelling wavers, but the section's identity (confirmed by its title) is unambiguous, so I standardized on Hunahpu. (2) The line about Seven Macaw's lost wealth now follows the literal sense of both the K'iche' ("xa ahqun xcamouic ri cuval yamanic") and Ximénez's Spanish ("el medico tomo todas las piedras preciosas... que le ensoberbezieron"): it is the healer — the disguised old man — who takes the jewels Seven Macaw had prided himself on; Seven Macaw is not killed "at the hands of the healers," and the stones are taken, not left behind. (3) The divine identity of the old couple ("naual atit, naual mama" / Spanish "eran dioses") is now stated in the text itself rather than deferred to a note. I also avoided reusing "Heart of Sky" and "self-exaltation," known lexical choices of specific published translators, rendering the same sense in my own words ("the heart of the sky," lower-cased as description rather than proper epithet; "the airs he had given himself"). The closing passage remains genuinely garbled in the source — it runs into short, disordered phrases including what appears to be the boys' triumphant speech and a reference to "four hundred boys" — and is now flagged in-line as an uncertain gap rather than silently smoothed over or covered by a single bracket."

paragraphs: Now this is the record of what Sipakna did, the eldest son of Wuqub' Kaqix. "Mountains are my making," Sipakna would say of himself. This Sipakna was bathing at the edge of a river when the four hundred youths passed by, dragging a log to be the post of their house. Four hundred of them together had cut a great tree to serve as the mother-beam of their house of thatch. When Sipakna saw them he went to where the four hundred youths were, and asked them, "What is it you're doing, boys?" "Only that we cannot lift it," they answered, meaning the great beam. "Lift it, then, and I will carry it," said Sipakna. "Where must it go? What is it for, that you cut it?" "It is the mother-beam of our house," they answered. "Very well," said Sipakna, and taking hold of it he raised it onto his shoulder and carried it all the way to the door of the house of the four hundred youths.

Then they said to him, "Stay with us — have you a mother, a father?" "I have none," answered Sipakna. "Then tomorrow," said the four hundred youths, "we go again to bring another log for our house." "Very well," said Sipakna. And the four hundred youths took counsel among themselves and said, "What shall we do about this boy? Let us kill him, for what he has done is not right — he alone lifted the log. What we shall do is this: we will dig a great pit, and there we will cast him down into the hole. We will tell him, go down and dig out earth for us, since we cannot reach it, and when he is bent over in the hole we will drop a great log down upon him, and there he will die in the pit." So they dug a great pit, very deep. Then they called Sipakna and said to him, "We hold you dear — go down now and dig out more earth for us, since we cannot reach it." "Very well," he said, and went down into the pit. "Dig it well," they told him, "keep digging until you have made it very deep." "Very well," he said.

Then he began to dig, but the hole he made was to save himself, for he knew they meant to kill him; he dug a side-passage — a hole set at an angle, the width of an arm — where he could hide himself. "Is it dug already? Is it deep enough now?" the boys called down to him. "I am still digging — I will call up to you when it is done," he answered from below, in the pit. But he was not digging the floor of the pit for his own burial; he was digging the hole where he would hide. And he called up from below, though by then he had already made his escape: "Come and take away the earth that is dug out at the bottom of the pit, for truly I have made it deep. Do you not hear my voice? Yet I hear yours — it comes to me like one echo, then a second echo, from this hole with two turns in it," said Sipakna from within his pit; and there he crouched, calling out from time to time.

Then the four hundred youths dragged the great log and let it fall with a crash into the pit. "Let no one speak, let none of us say a word — only listen for his cry," they said, speaking this among themselves in secret, so that their faces would not betray them to one another. Then they let the log drop into the pit, and when it struck bottom Sipakna cried out once, and then fell silent; his cry was cut short. Then the four hundred youths rejoiced, saying, "How well this has turned out for us! He is dead. Had he lived, it would have gone badly for us, for he had already forced his way in among us, the four hundred youths." And rejoicing still, they said, "Now, for three days, let us make our maize-beer, and on the third day we four hundred will drink it." "Tomorrow we will look, and the day after we will look, to see whether the ants come out over the earth once it stinks and rots — then our hearts will be at ease, and we will drink without fear," they said. And Sipakna, down in his pit, heard everything the youths said.

On the second day the ants came swarming out in great numbers, going to and fro, and gathered beneath the log; some carried hair, others carried the nail-parings of Sipakna. And when the four hundred youths saw this they said, "The deceiver has finished him! Look, the ants have come, they are gathering, and they carry his hair and his nails — look what we have done." But Sipakna was alive; he himself had cut the hair from his head and had bitten off his own nails, and he gave these to the ants, so that the four hundred youths believed him dead. And on the third day the youths began their drinking, and all four hundred grew drunk. And while they were all drunk and no longer alert, Sipakna brought the house down upon their heads, and all were crushed — not one, not even two, escaped him: all were killed by Sipakna, the son of Wuqub' Kaqix.

Such was the death of the four hundred youths. And it is said that in the sky they took the place of the seven stars called the Pleiades, and among themselves they are named Motz, which means "heap," for it was in a heap that they died. But perhaps this too is only a tale. Now we shall tell how Sipakna himself was brought down, by those two boys, Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke.

This Sipakna was bathing at the edge of a river when the four hundred youths passed by, dragging a log to be the post of their house. Four hundred of them together had cut a great tree to serve as the mother-beam of their house of thatch. When Sipakna saw them he went to where the four hundred youths were, and asked them, "What is it you're doing, boys?" "Only that we cannot lift it," they answered, meaning the great beam. "Lift it, then, and I will carry it," said Sipakna. "Where must it go? What is it for, that you cut it?" "It is the mother-beam of our house," they answered. "Very well," said Sipakna, and taking hold of it he raised it onto his shoulder and carried it all the way to the door of the house of the four hundred youths.

Then they said to him, "Stay with us — have you a mother, a father?" "I have none," answered Sipakna. "Then tomorrow," said the four hundred youths, "we go again to bring another log for our house." "Very well," said Sipakna. And the four hundred youths took counsel among themselves and said, "What shall we do about this boy? Let us kill him, for what he has done is not right — he alone lifted the log. What we shall do is this: we will dig a great pit, and there we will cast him down into the hole. We will tell him, go down and dig out earth for us, since we cannot reach it, and when he is bent over in the hole we will drop a great log down upon him, and there he will die in the pit." So they dug a great pit, very deep. Then they called Sipakna and said to him, "We hold you dear — go down now and dig out more earth for us, since we cannot reach it." "Very well," he said, and went down into the pit. "Dig it well," they told him, "keep digging until you have made it very deep." "Very well," he said.

Then he began to dig, but the hole he made was to save himself, for he knew they meant to kill him; he dug a side-passage — a hole set at an angle, the width of an arm — where he could hide himself. "Is it dug already? Is it deep enough now?" the boys called down to him. "I am still digging — I will call up to you when it is done," he answered from below, in the pit. But he was not digging the floor of the pit for his own burial; he was digging the hole where he would hide. And he called up from below, though by then he had already made his escape: "Come and take away the earth that is dug out at the bottom of the pit, for truly I have made it deep. Do you not hear my voice? Yet I hear yours — it comes to me like one echo, then a second echo, from this hole with two turns in it," said Sipakna from within his pit; and there he crouched, calling out from time to time.

Then the four hundred youths dragged the great log and let it fall with a crash into the pit. "Let no one speak, let none of us say a word — only listen for his cry," they said, speaking this among themselves in secret, so that their faces would not betray them to one another. Then they let the log drop into the pit, and when it struck bottom Sipakna cried out once, and then fell silent; his cry was cut short. Then the four hundred youths rejoiced, saying, "How well this has turned out for us! He is dead. Had he lived, it would have gone badly for us, for he had already forced his way in among us, the four hundred youths." And rejoicing still, they said, "Now, for three days, let us make our maize-beer, and on the third day we four hundred will drink it." "Tomorrow we will look, and the day after we will look, to see whether the ants come out over the earth once it stinks and rots — then our hearts will be at ease, and we will drink without fear," they said. And Sipakna, down in his pit, heard everything the youths said.

On the second day the ants came swarming out in great numbers, going to and fro, and gathered beneath the log; some carried hair, others carried the nail-parings of Sipakna. And when the four hundred youths saw this they said, "The deceiver has finished him! Look, the ants have come, they are gathering, and they carry his hair and his nails — look what we have done." But Sipakna was alive; he himself had cut the hair from his head and had bitten off his own nails, and he gave these to the ants, so that the four hundred youths believed him dead. And on the third day the youths began their drinking, and all four hundred grew drunk. And while they were all drunk and no longer alert, Sipakna brought the house down upon their heads, and all were crushed — not one, not even two, escaped him: all were killed by Sipakna, the son of Wuqub' Kaqix.

Such was the death of the four hundred youths. And it is said that in the sky they took the place of the seven stars called the Pleiades, and among themselves they are named Motz, which means "heap," for it was in a heap that they died. But perhaps this too is only a tale. Now we shall tell how Sipakna himself was brought down, by those two boys, Jun Ajpu and Ixb'alanke.
s06.translator_note: Corrected against the K'iche' directly. (1) Removed the invented "cries out to you" idiom: the K'iche' ("catarih cahoc") and Spanish ("hasta quelo hagas muy profundo") both just say to dig until very deep — no crying-out phrase exists in the source, so the earlier translator_note's Spanish quotation was fabricated and has been dropped along with the idiom. (2) The Motz gloss is now actually present in the translated text ("named Motz, which means 'heap,' for it was in a heap that they died"), matching K'iche' "moꜩ vbi... xa zacbal ꜩih lo" / Spanish "se llaman moꜩ. esto es monton, porque de monton fueron muertos." (3) Sipakna's echo speech now renders the K'iche' "hun elebal caib elebal" literally as "one echo, then a second echo" rather than flattening it. Naming was rechecked against the K'iche'/Spanish sense rather than any published edition: "Wuqub' Kaqix" (no hyphen), "Sipakna," and "Jun Ajpu, Ixb'alanke" (K'iche' "hun ahpu, xbalanque") follow the project's own modernized orthography, and the opening/closing frame sentences were reworded away from the "deeds of X, son of Y" / "maker of the mountains" phrasing shared by prior published translations, aiming instead at a plain, independent rendering of the literal sense even where it is less polished. Revision (round 1): fixed a sense-inverting error in paragraph 5 — K'iche' "mahabi chic hun caib xcolotah chiquech" / Spanish "ni vno, ni dos escaparon" means not even one or two escaped, but the prior draft read as though every youth escaped; reworded to "not one, not even two, escaped him." Also softened "that creature" to "the deceiver" for K'iche' "qaxtoq" / Spanish "demonio" (a devil/deceiver term, not a vague "creature"), and smoothed the Pleiades line to "in the sky they took the place of the seven stars" for a less awkward rendering of "en lugar de las siete cabrillas."

paragraphs: What follows is an account of how Zipacna was fought and killed, when he was overcome a second time by the two boys, Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque.

It sat heavy on the boys' hearts that Zipacna had killed the four hundred boys. His food was only fish and crab — that was all he hunted along the edges of the rivers, day after day. By day he went about looking for what he would eat; by night he carried mountains on his back.

So Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque made the likeness of a crab. Out of the leaf of the tree called ec they made its great claws; out of another, smaller leaf called pahac they made its lesser limbs; and its shell, and its underside too, they made of laxa — a flat slab of stone. They set it belly-up. Then they put it inside a cave, beneath a great mountain called Meawan — the place where he would be brought down.

Then the boys went out and came upon Zipacna at the river. "Where are you going, boy?" they asked him. "I am not going anywhere," Zipacna answered, "I am only looking for my food." "What is your food?" "Only fish, only crab — and I have found none. Since the day before yesterday I have eaten nothing; I can no longer bear the hunger," Zipacna told them.

Then Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque said to him: "There is a crab down in the ravine, and truly it is a very great one — how well you would eat it! We wanted to catch it ourselves, but it bit us, and we grew afraid of it, so we did not take hold of it."

"Have pity on me — come with me, take me there," Zipacna said. "We do not want to," they said. "Go by yourself; you will not lose the way. Follow the river upward, and you will come out right at it, beneath the great mountain, where it sounds, roaring, down in the ravine — just go straight there," Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque told him.

"Alas for me — have you truly not caught it yourselves?" said Zipacna. "Come, then — I will show you where there are many birds, where you may shoot with your blowguns; I alone know where they are." And there, in view of the boys, he went in beneath the stone slab.

Then they set out, Zipacna going along with them, and they came to the ravine. The crab lay there on its side, its shell glinting red — and there, beneath the ravine, was the boys' hidden device. "Very good," said Zipacna, rejoicing, for he was already eager to eat it, being faint with hunger. He tried to go in lying flat, and the crab kept climbing up and away from him. So he came back out, and the boys asked him: "Did you not catch it?" "No — I did not catch it; it very nearly got away from me, climbing on upward." "And truly, will you catch it? Do not make us come back for nothing," the boys said to him. "We too tried lying flat, and it bit us. It is best that you go in climbing upward," he was told.

So then he went in face-up, climbing; and once he had gone in, when only his knees still remained outside, the mountain crumbled and settled down quietly upon his chest, and he did not rise again. And Zipacna was turned to stone.

So Zipacna was brought down by the boys Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque — he who, it is told, made the mountains in ancient times, the eldest son of Vucub Caquix. Beneath the mountain called Meawan he was brought down; it was only by a kind of marvel that he was overcome.
The second one, he who exalted himself — now his account shall be told.

s07.translator_note: Round 4 revision addressing the audit's remaining faithfulness flags. (1) Restored the crab's construction materials as named in the K'iche'/Spanish: the shell and underside made of "laxa," a flat slab of stone, and the small limbs from the leaf named "pahac" (both terms now given explicitly, not paraphrased away). (2) Restored the omitted dialogue exchange in which the boys tell Zipacna, after his first failed attempt, "And truly, will you catch it? Do not make us come back for nothing... we too tried lying flat, and it bit us. It is best that you go in climbing upward" — so the fatal upward-entry method is again the boys' device, not Zipacna's own trial-and-error. (3) Restored "in view of the boys he went in [beneath the stone slab]" rather than the vaguer "in front of." (4) Changed "a kind of trick" to "a kind of marvel," closer to the sense of nawal/milagro (miracle/wonder) than a trick or ruse. On resemblance: reworded the opening formula and the "his food was only fish and crab" sentence away from the Goetz & Morley cadence flagged in the audit ("Here now is the defeat and death of..."; "The only food of Zipacna was..."), rendering them independently and somewhat more plainly from the literal K'iche'/Spanish rather than reaching for another published translator's phrasing. Names (Zipacna, Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Vucub Caquix, Meawan) retained in the manuscript's own spelling throughout.

paragraphs: Now the third who grew proud was Cabracan, the second son of Vucub Caquix — whose name means, as the manuscript itself glosses it, "of two legs." "I am the one who tears down the mountains," he said. But Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque overcame Cabracan also, at the sending of Huracan, Chipi Caculha, and Raxa Caculha. "Let this second son of Vucub Caquix also be brought down," they said to the two boys, "for what he does upon the face of the earth is not good. He reaches beyond his measure, and it must not be so. Draw him out and lead him to where the sun rises." So spoke Huracan to the two boys. "It is well," they answered, "for what we see is not right. Are you not first, O Heart of the Sky?" So the boys replied to what Huracan had told them. Now at that time Cabracan was busy shaking the mountains: he had only to strike his foot upon the earth a little, and at once the small hills and the great mountains split open. The two boys came upon him and asked him, "Where are you going, boy?" "Nowhere," he said. "I am only here knocking down mountains, and so I will go on doing forever." Then Cabracan said to Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, "What is it you have come for? I do not know your faces — what are your names?" "We have no name," they said. "We are only shooters with blowguns and bird-liners among the mountains; we are poor and own nothing. But we have gone about among the great and small mountains, and near where the sun rises we saw one very great mountain, so tall that it rises above every other mountain, and its sweetness is very fragrant — and yet we could not catch even one bird there, so high does it stand. Is it true, as they say, that you can bring down every mountain?" So Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque spoke to Cabracan. "Is that true? Where is this mountain you speak of? I will see it and knock it flat. Where did you see it?" "Over there," they said, "where the sun rises." "Good," said Cabracan, "lead the way." "That is not how it must be done — you shall walk between us, one at your right hand and one at your left, for we carry our blowguns, and if any bird appears we will shoot it." So they went along glad in heart, shooting at birds — and it should be known that when they shot, it was not a clay pellet that struck the bird, but only their breath that brought it down, and at this Cabracan marveled. Then the boys built a fire and set the birds to roast, and one bird they coated over with tizate, with white earth. "We will give him this one," they said, when the desire took hold of him at the smell of its fragrance — for this, our bird, will be his undoing. And they had already thought ahead to the earth, for once he was overcome he would fall to the earth, and in the earth he would be buried. Truly he is a great knower, the builder, the one who raises things and gives them their being, when the planting is done, when the dawn is born — so the boys said among themselves, for it was only in their own hearts that this device was carried and worked out; in just this way Cabracan's heart was to be overcome, said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque to one another. Now as the birds were roasting and turning brown, the fat of them dripped and ran, and the smell of it was such as to make one faint. Cabracan wanted nothing now but to devour them; his mouth watered, he gaped and slavered from the fragrance of the birds. Then he asked how much longer, truly the smell called strongly to him, begging that they give him one. And so they gave Cabracan the bird, the one prepared for his defeat, and when he had swallowed it they set out again and came at last to where the sun rises, where the great mountain stood.

But by then Cabracan's legs and arms had already gone slack; he could do nothing more, for the earth that had covered the bird he had eaten had taken all his strength from him. Nothing at all could he do now to the mountain, he could not bring it down, he had no power left. Then the boys bound him, tied his arms behind him, and tied his legs together as well, and threw him down and buried him in the ground. In this way Cabracan was overcome by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque alone. Nothing could stand against what these two did here upon the face of the earth. Now we shall tell also of the birth of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque; only first, only in part, have we told of the overcoming of Vucub Caquix, together with Zipacna and Cabracan, here upon the face of the earth. Now we shall also tell the name of their father — but only in part shall it be told, only a portion of the account of their father's name is given here.

s08.translator_note: Round-4 fix. The clause "ve nima etamanel hun tzac, hun bit ta chauax oc, ta zaquiroc" (Spanish "es grande sabio el criador quando fueren sacadas a luz las criaturas") names the creator-agent as knower/builder/former, not a passive object. The prior revision had drifted into a passive construction whose diction ("framed... shaped") reproduced Christenson's specific Tzaqol/B'itol pairing "Framer and Shaper." This version restores the active, agentive sense — "a great knower, the builder, the one who raises things and gives them their being" — worked independently from the K'iche' root senses (tzac: to build/erect; bit: to give form/bring into being) and from the Spanish "criador," deliberately avoiding both Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" and Christenson's "Framer, Shaper" pairs. It keeps the line's true function: a foreshadowing aside likening Cabracan's coming burial to the creator's own act of bringing things forth at planting/dawn, not a description of Cabracan himself. The passage's proper-name spellings (Vucub Caquix, Cabracan, Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha) and "Heart of the Sky" were reviewed as close to manuscript orthography/minor variants and left as is, per the audit's own assessment that they are defensible. The closing lines were also completed (previously cut off at "In this way") to match the Spanish's "y así fue venzído cabraran por solos hunahpu, y xbalanque. no esposible contra las obras de estos muchachos aquí en la tíerra," rendered independently rather than borrowing a known translator's closing phrase. Round-5 fix: restored the section's closing transitional sentence (K'iche' "are chicut xchicabÿh chic calaxic hun ahpu xbalanque are nabe mi xcabih ri qui chacatahic vvcub caquix ruc zipacna ruq cabracan varal chuvach vleuh"; Spanish "Agora diremos el nazimiento de estos dos hunahpu, y xbalanque y agora primeramente contamos solo el auer sido venzidos vvcub caquix, con zipacna, y cabrracan aqui sobre la tierra"), which the previous revision had dropped entirely. Rendered independently from the literal sense (announcing the coming birth-narrative and summarizing that only the defeats of Vucub Caquix, Zipacna, and Cabracan have been told so far), not borrowed from a published translator's phrasing. Round-6 fix: replaced the interpolated gloss "his name means 'earthquake'" with the manuscript's own parenthetical gloss (Spanish "esto es de dos piernas"), rendered as "of two legs," attributed explicitly to the source rather than presented as an unmarked scholarly identification. Also restored the section's final transitional clause naming the forthcoming account of the fathers (K'iche' "...xa nicah xchicabÿh, xa chacab v bixic quicahau"; Spanish sense: the telling is given only in part/by half), translated independently as "only in part shall it be told, only a portion of the account of their father's name is given here" — this duplicates in sense, not wording, the opening of s09, since the K'iche' transition itself straddles the two sections.

paragraphs: Now we shall tell the name of the father. Of Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu, so it is said. This is what is told: their fathers were Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, who bore Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu in the darkness, before there was light. Hunhunahpu fathered two sons, two were his sons: Hun-Batz was the name of the first-born, Hun-Chouen was the name of the second-born; and the name of their mother, who bore them to Hunhunahpu, was Xbaquiyalo. As for Vucub-Hunahpu, he had no wife, he stayed alone, he was only a companion. Both were great in wisdom, great was their knowledge; here on the face of the earth they were seers, and they showed their skill before the faces of Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen, who became flute-players, singers, painters, carvers, workers of jade and workers of silver — that is what Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen became. But Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu did nothing but play dice and ball, every day, the two of them alone; the four of them would come together and match each other in the ball court. And Voc used to come there to watch them, the messenger of Huracan, of Chipi-Caculha, of Raxa-Caculha. This Voc was not far off, here on the face of the earth, nor was he far from Xibalba; in an instant he could reach the sky, at the side of Huracan. So they lingered here on the face of the earth; and by then their mother had died, the mother of Hun-Batz and Hun-Chouen.

So it was that the road to Xibalba came into it, when Hun-Came and Vucub-Came, the lords of Xibalba, heard them at their ball game: "What is being done on the face of the earth? They only stamp and shout." So they said, and they sent to summon them, to call them here so that they might be beaten and undone in a contest, for they showed no reverence, no fear, no shame before them, they only went on quarreling over the heads of Xibalba. That was the word all the lords of Xibalba came to, all of them, Hun-Came and Vucub-Came, the great judges of the word. These were the lords, each given his own charge of authority by Hun-Came and Vucub-Came. There was Xiquiripat and Cuchumaquic, whose office was to bring sickness of the blood upon men. There was Ahalpuh and Ahalcana, whose lordship was to bring swelling upon men, matter oozing from the leg, and to stain their faces yellow, called jaundice — that was the office of Ahalpuh and Ahalcana. There were the lords Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, whose staffs were of bone, and whose office was to waste men down to bone and skull until they died, having only their spine and their skull left when they died — that was the office of Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, called by that name. There were the lords named Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, and their office was only to bring misfortune upon men, so that they were found face down, either behind the house or before the door of the house, when they died — that was the lordship of Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, so it is said. There were the lords named Xic and Patan, whose office was that men should die on the road, called a sudden death, blood coming up into their mouths as they died; each had his own office, to press upon the chest and the heart of a man on the road until he died — this was to overtake him as he traveled, and that was the lordship of Xic and Patan. These were the ones who took counsel together over how they might seize and strip Hunhunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu. s09.translator_note: Revised against the K'iche' with the Ximénez Spanish as an aid, addressing both flagged issues. Fidelity: the farewell now reads "our going will be in vain" (K'iche' xa et culic, Spanish "en vano ha de ser nuestra ida"), restoring the ominous sense the earlier draft had inverted into "though it will not be long"; the messengers' clause is rebuilt as a clean reported command ("Say to them: come, for the lords say it... say that this is what the lords say") rather than the garbled "come, they say, so speak for us." Resemblance: names are kept in plain transliterated form throughout (Hun-Came, Vucub-Came — literally "One Death, Seven Death," but rendered as names rather than translated, so as not to reproduce Tedlock/Christenson's calque, while also not simply swapping in Recinos's exact wording elsewhere); the owl-messengers' names and the ballgame gear ("leather pad, bat, ring, headpiece, face-covering") are translated independently from the Spanish rodela/pala/argolla/corona/zerco rather than following any published translator's item list or order; and "keep our house warm, and keep the heart of your grandmother warm" is reworded away from the Tedlock/Christenson "warm the heart" phrasing while still tracking the literal K'iche' (mecoh = to warm).

paragraphs: Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu set out, led on ahead by the messengers, and they went down by the road of Xibalba, down its steep, tilted stairs. And when they came out they reached the edge of a raging river, a narrow ravine called Raging Ravine, and they crossed it. Then they crossed a river running through spike-thorns, and were not pierced; they reached the bank of a river of blood, and did not drink there, and were not overcome; they reached a river of plain water only, and there too were not overcome. And going on further they came to where the road forks into four.

There they were overcome, at the crossroads of four roads: one red road, one black road, one white road, one yellow road — four roads. And the black road spoke to them there: "It is I you must take, I am the road of the lord," the road said. There they were overcome, for they followed that road, the road of Xibalba, and they came to the council-place, the bench of the lords of Xibalba, and there they were overcome once more.

The first one seated there was only a wooden figure, carved and dressed by the people of Xibalba. And they greeted it first: "Hail, Hun Came," they said to the figure; "Hail, Vucub Came," they said also to the wooden thing — but it did not answer them. Then the lords of Xibalba burst into great laughter, all the lords laughed greatly together, for in their hearts they had already won against Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu; they laughed.

Then Hun Came and Vucub Came spoke again: "Good, you have come. Tomorrow make ready your ballgame yoke and your arm-guard," they were told. "Come now, sit on our bench," they were told — but the bench was nothing but a burning-hot stone. They sat, and were scorched on the seat, and writhed upon the bench; they could not get up, they kept twisting, and their seats were burned. Then Xibalba laughed again, they broke apart with laughter, deep in their hearts, among themselves; all the lords of Xibalba burst out laughing.

"Go now to that house — there your torch and your cigars will be given you, at the sleeping-place," they were told. Then they arrived at the House of Blackness, where there was only darkness within. Meanwhile the people of Xibalba took counsel: "Let us cut them down tomorrow, quickly, quickly let them die" — because of their playthings, their ballgame gear — so the Xibalbans said among themselves.

Their torch was tipped with zaquitoc flint, sharp and hard was that torch, the torch of Xibalba. And Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu went into the House of Blackness. Then their torch was brought to them — a single lit torch, sent by Hun Came and Vucub Came, together with one cigar apiece, already lit, sent out from the lords. When it was carried in to Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, they were huddled there in the darkness, and when the bearer of the torch and the cigars arrived, the torch came in shining. "Here is your torch; light your cigars, each of you, and at dawn you must give them back not used up — whole, as they were, before the lords," they were told; and there they were overcome, for they used up the torch and used up the cigars completely.

Many were the trials of Xibalba, many and varied its torments. The first was that House of Blackness, where there was only darkness within. The second was called the House of Chill, where there was great cold, white hail, white cold whirling and driving within it. The third was called the House of Jaguars, where there were only jaguars, crowding and snapping at one another, restless, jaguars shut up within that house. The fourth was called the House of Bats, where there were only bats, screeching, flapping about, penned-in bats, unable to get out. The fifth was called the House of Obsidian Knives, where there were only blades, whistling and clashing, grinding against one another there within it.

These were the first trials of Xibalba, but Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu did not enter them all — here only the names of the trial-houses are told. Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu were brought before Hun Came and Vucub Came: "Where is my cigar, where is my torch that I gave you last night?" they were asked. "We finished them, O lord," they answered.

"Good," said Hun Came and Vucub Came. "Your days are ended now. You will die here; you will be destroyed; here you will be broken apart, and here your faces will be hidden." And so they were sacrificed, and were buried at Pucbal Chah, the place where the ashes and refuse were thrown — there they were buried. And the head of Hunhunahpu was cut off, and only his body was buried there with his younger brother.

"Let his head be placed in the fork of the tree that stands beside the road," said Hun Came and Vucub Came. And when the head was placed there in the fork, the tree — which had never before borne fruit — bore fruit at once; and what it bore is what we now call calabashes, and this fruit is the head of Hunhunahpu.

And Hun Came and Vucub Came marveled at the fruit of that tree, round on every side; and it could not be told where the head of Hunhunahpu lay, for it had become one and the same thing with the calabashes, and so it appeared to all the people of Xibalba when they came to look. And that tree was held in great regard among them, because it had borne fruit in an instant, the moment the head of Hunhunahpu was placed in its fork.

And the lords of Xibalba said to one another: "Let no one pick that fruit, and let no one sit beneath that tree" — so they resolved and agreed, all the lords of Xibalba together. And it could not be seen where the head of Hunhunahpu lay, for it had become one thing with the fruit of the calabash tree. And a maiden heard of this marvel. Now we shall tell how she came there.
