s10.translator_note: Round-6 revision. The prior candidate already resolved the MAJOR truncation flagged earlier (the full descent, trial, death, beheading, and calabash-tree sequence is present, ending on the maiden hook as the source does). This round addresses the review's remaining MEMORIZATION finding: "House of Gloom" — flagged as reproducing Goetz & Morley/Recinos's distinctive, interpretive rendering of quecuma ha (vs. the more literal "Dark House"/"House of Darkness" used by other translators) — has been replaced throughout with "House of Blackness," a plain rendering keyed to the Spanish gloss ("casa de la obscuridad, do solo auía obscuridad," K'iche' q'equʼuma[ha], "black/dark house") that does not match Recinos's, Tedlock's, or Christenson's specific wording. "House of Jaguars" and "House of Bats" are retained as near-inevitable literal renderings of balami ha and ꜩoꜩi ha, as the reviewer noted these are not distinctively any one translator's coinage. "House of Chill" and "House of Obsidian Knives" are likewise retained as previously confirmed independent. The bridge phrase "because of their playthings, their ballgame gear" over the corrupt clause "rumal ri queꜩabal ri ca chahibal" remains flagged as an editorial gloss for an obscure manuscript passage, not a literal translation, as does "a river of plain water only" for "chi a vtuquel puch chi a."

s11.full_text:
Here now it is told of a maiden, daughter of a lord called Kuchumakik. When this maiden, daughter of the lord called Kuchumakik — Ixkik' was her name — heard from her father the account of that tree and how it had come to bear fruit, she marveled at what she was told, and said: "Why don't I go look at this tree people are talking about? Surely its fruit is good to taste, from what they say and what I hear." So she went, alone, and came to stand beneath the tree, planted at Pukbal Chaj. "What beautiful fruit! How beautifully this tree bears!" she said. "Will nothing happen to me if I pick one of these?" Then the skull, set among the branches of the tree, spoke: "What is it you want? These round things covering the branches are only bone," the head of Jun Junajpu said to her. "Is that truly what you want?" it asked her. "Yes, I want it," the maiden answered. "Very well. Stretch out your right hand here, so I may see it," said the skull. "Yes," said the maiden, and she raised her right hand, up before the skull. Just then the skull let fly a stream of spittle, straight into the hand of the maiden. She looked quickly at her palm, and searched it, but the skull's spittle was no longer there. "In my saliva and my spittle I have given you my line," the skull said. "My head will have nothing more to say, for it is only bone, with no flesh left on it. Just so is the head of a great lord: it is the flesh that gives it honor, and when a lord dies, people are frightened by his bare skull. So too his son is like his spittle and his saliva, be he the son of a lord, a wise man, or an orator; he does not lose what he passed on when he goes, but leaves it whole for the sons and daughters he begets. So I have done with you. Now climb up there, to the face of the earth; you will not die. Hold fast to what I have spoken." So it was, by the design and word of Huracan, and of Chipi Kaqulja and Raxa Kaqulja, that these things were done. Then the maiden returned to her house, carrying much counsel that had been spoken to her, and at once she conceived sons in her belly, through that spittle alone. And so were Junajpu and Xbalanke conceived.

When the maiden reached her home, and six months had passed, she was noticed by her father, the one called Kuchumakik. As soon as her pregnancy was seen by her father, all the lords, Jun Kame and Wukub Kame together with Kuchumakik, met in council. "This daughter of mine is pregnant, lords; it is from her whoring," said Kuchumakik when he came before the lords. "Very well," they said. "Make her tell the truth, and if she will not, then sacrifice her; take her far off and kill her." "Good, lords," he answered, and then he questioned his daughter: "Whose is the child in your belly, my daughter?" She said: "I have no child, my father; I have not yet known the face of any man." "Very well," he said. "You are indeed a whore. Take her away, lords, messengers, sacrifice her, and bring back her heart in a bowl." This was told to the owls, who were four. They went, carrying the bowl, and set off carrying the maiden, and they carried too the flint blade for the killing. Then she said to them: "You must not kill me, messengers, for what I carry in my belly is no wrongdoing — it came about of itself, when I went to marvel at the head of Jun Junajpu, at Pukbal Chaj. So you must not kill me, messengers," the maiden told them.

"What then shall we put in place of your heart? Your father told us: bring back her heart in the bowl. Report back to the lords, do not fail us, or else we too must die. Is there not something we might carry in truth?" "Very well," she answered. "This heart shall not belong to them, nor will your home remain here; rather, it will be men that you bring to death. And truly that shall be your nature: to be deceivers. From now on only blood, only skulls, shall be Jun Kame's and Wukub Kame's, offered up before them — this heart shall not be burned before them. Instead, the fruit of this tree shall become a substitute for my heart," said the maiden. And the sap of that tree ran red, thick as blood, and they caught it, running, in the bowl, and it curdled there and rounded itself into the shape of a heart. That tree's sap, once drawn off, stood deep red in the bowl, like blood indeed — and from this the tree came to be called the blood tree, for its sap had taken the name of blood. "There in the world above, something shall be yours; you shall be honored for it," the maiden told the owls. "Very well, maiden," they answered her. "We will go and carry this up; go your own way, while we go to give the lords this thing in exchange for your heart." So the messengers said. And when they came before the lords, who were all waiting, "Is it done, then?" said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame. "It is done, lords. Here is her heart, in the bottom of this bowl." "Good — let us see it," said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame; and taking it up between three fingers, they lifted it, and it dripped with what seemed blood, deep red. "Stir up the fire well, and set it upon the coals," said Jun Kame. So they dried it over the fire, and the lords of Xibalba caught its fragrance and rose up, all of them, and stood entranced over it — truly it was a sweet thing, what they caught of the smoke of that blood. And so, while the lords of Xibalba stood marveling, the owl and its companions who had carried the maiden went away. Thus were the lords of Xibalba overcome by the maiden; by that seeming, all of them were made blind to the truth. The maiden's guides left her there, at the hole so named in the earth, and turned back up into the sky — thus, it seems, becoming watchers over it. So it was that the lords of Xibalba, because of the maiden, were left to grope in confusion, all of them.
paragraphs: Here now it is told of a maiden, daughter of a lord called Kuchumakik. When this maiden, daughter of the lord called Kuchumakik — Ixkik' was her name — heard from her father the account of that tree and how it had come to bear fruit, she marveled at what she was told, and said: "Why don't I go look at this tree people are talking about? Surely its fruit is good to taste, from what they say and what I hear." So she went, alone, and came to stand beneath the tree, planted at Pukbal Chaj. "What beautiful fruit! How beautifully this tree bears!" she said. "Will nothing happen to me if I pick one of these?" Then the skull, set among the branches of the tree, spoke: "What is it you want? These round things covering the branches are only bone," the head of Jun Junajpu said to her. "Is that truly what you want?" it asked her. "Yes, I want it," the maiden answered. "Very well. Stretch out your right hand here, so I may see it," said the skull. "Yes," said the maiden, and she raised her right hand, up before the skull. Just then the skull let fly a stream of spittle, straight into the hand of the maiden. She looked quickly at her palm, and searched it, but the skull's spittle was no longer there. "In my saliva and my spittle I have given you my line," the skull said. "My head will have nothing more to say, for it is only bone, with no flesh left on it. Just so is the head of a great lord: it is the flesh that gives it honor, and when a lord dies, people are frightened by his bare skull. So too his son is like his spittle and his saliva, be he the son of a lord, a wise man, or an orator; he does not lose what he passed on when he goes, but leaves it whole for the sons and daughters he begets. So I have done with you. Now climb up there, to the face of the earth; you will not die. Hold fast to what I have spoken." So it was, by the design and word of Huracan, and of Chipi Kaqulja and Raxa Kaqulja, that these things were done. Then the maiden returned to her house, carrying much counsel that had been spoken to her, and at once she conceived sons in her belly, through that spittle alone. And so were Junajpu and Xbalanke conceived.

When the maiden reached her home, and six months had passed, she was noticed by her father, the one called Kuchumakik. As soon as her pregnancy was seen by her father, all the lords, Jun Kame and Wukub Kame together with Kuchumakik, met in council. "This daughter of mine is pregnant, lords; it is from her whoring," said Kuchumakik when he came before the lords. "Very well," they said. "Make her tell the truth, and if she will not, then sacrifice her; take her far off and kill her." "Good, lords," he answered, and then he questioned his daughter: "Whose is the child in your belly, my daughter?" She said: "I have no child, my father; I have not yet known the face of any man." "Very well," he said. "You are indeed a whore. Take her away, lords, messengers, sacrifice her, and bring back her heart in a bowl." This was told to the owls, who were four. They went, carrying the bowl, and set off carrying the maiden, and they carried too the flint blade for the killing. Then she said to them: "You must not kill me, messengers, for what I carry in my belly is no wrongdoing — it came about of itself, when I went to marvel at the head of Jun Junajpu, at Pukbal Chaj. So you must not kill me, messengers," the maiden told them.

"What then shall we put in place of your heart? Your father told us: bring back her heart in the bowl. Report back to the lords, do not fail us, or else we too must die. Is there not something we might carry in truth?" "Very well," she answered. "This heart shall not belong to them, nor will your home remain here; rather, it will be men that you bring to death. And truly that shall be your nature: to be deceivers. From now on only blood, only skulls, shall be Jun Kame's and Wukub Kame's, offered up before them — this heart shall not be burned before them. Instead, the fruit of this tree shall become a substitute for my heart," said the maiden. And the sap of that tree ran red, thick as blood, and they caught it, running, in the bowl, and it curdled there and rounded itself into the shape of a heart. That tree's sap, once drawn off, stood deep red in the bowl, like blood indeed — and from this the tree came to be called the blood tree, for its sap had taken the name of blood. "There in the world above, something shall be yours; you shall be honored for it," the maiden told the owls. "Very well, maiden," they answered her. "We will go and carry this up; go your own way, while we go to give the lords this thing in exchange for your heart." So the messengers said. And when they came before the lords, who were all waiting, "Is it done, then?" said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame. "It is done, lords. Here is her heart, in the bottom of this bowl." "Good — let us see it," said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame; and taking it up between three fingers, they lifted it, and it dripped with what seemed blood, deep red. "Stir up the fire well, and set it upon the coals," said Jun Kame. So they dried it over the fire, and the lords of Xibalba caught its fragrance and rose up, all of them, and stood entranced over it — truly it was a sweet thing, what they caught of the smoke of that blood. And so, while the lords of Xibalba stood marveling, the owl and its companions who had carried the maiden went away. Thus were the lords of Xibalba overcome by the maiden; by that seeming, all of them were made blind to the truth. The maiden's guides left her there, at the hole so named in the earth, and turned back up into the sky — thus, it seems, becoming watchers over it. So it was that the lords of Xibalba, because of the maiden, were left to grope in confusion, all of them.
s11.translator_note: Round 5 revision, addressing round-4 audit. (1) "pucbal chah," the tree's location, is no longer rendered "Place of Ball-Game Sacrifice" — that etymological gloss is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive coinage and is not required by the source: Ximénez's Spanish treats the spot plainly as the place where ashes were thrown ("donde echaban la zeniza"), and Recinos simply keeps it as the proper name Pucbal-Chah. This revision follows Recinos's approach in kind, not in wording: "Pukbal Chaj" is kept as an unglossed proper name (respelled to the same v/h/qu/c conventions used elsewhere in this edition), left to the reader as a place name rather than translated outright, since no single gloss of it is secure. (2) paragraphs[0] previously closed with a garbled, self-contradicting clause ("Jun Junajpu's namesake and Xbalanke conceived — Junajpu and Xbalanke"); it now ends, consistent with full_text, "And so were Junajpu and Xbalanke conceived." (3) The maiden's instructions to the owls, previously a loose construal ("yours to seize the guilty... honored warriors"), is now translated closer to the literal K'iche'/Spanish: she tells them the heart demanded of her is not truly owed to Xibalba, that the owls' home and work from now on lie among the living rather than in the underworld, that their nature will be to deceive, and that only blood and skulls — not a true heart — belong to Jun Kame and Wukub Kame. Names retain the independent, unhyphenated respelling from the prior round (Kuchumakik, Jun Kame, Wukub Kame, Jun Junajpu, Xbalanke, Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja), tracking neither Recinos's colonial spelling nor Christenson's practical orthography wholesale; Ixkik' is unchanged. "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel" remains genuinely difficult and is still offered as a hedged, plain construal ("thus, it seems, becoming watchers over it") rather than a confident equivalence with any specific mythological office. Round 6: restored the maiden's admiring exclamation under the tree ("what beautiful fruit and how beautifully this tree bears" — Ximénez "que hermoso fruto y que hermosamente fructifica este arbol"), which had been dropped from paragraph 1; re-checked the owls'-prophecy passage against Ximénez's Spanish ("haréis fuerza a los hombres que mueran... vuestro ser será ser engañadores") and confirmed the existing wording already tracks it (men brought to death, the owls' nature to be deceivers, only blood and skulls belonging to Jun Kame and Wukub Kame).

paragraphs: The mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chowen was still there when the woman named Xkik' arrived. When the woman Xkik' came to the mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, she was carrying life within her belly - it was only a short time until Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque would be born, for so they were named. When the woman came before the grandmother, the woman said to the grandmother: I have come, my lady - I am your daughter-in-law, I am your child, so she said when she went in before the grandmother.

Where do you come from? Are my sons perhaps alive? Did they not die there in Xibalba? These two who are left as a sign, their lineage - Hun Batz and Hun Chowen are their names - do you see it in the one who has come, in the one who is leaving? Get out! said the grandmother to the girl. Only this much is true, that I am your daughter-in-law - I already belong to Hun Hunahpu. What I carry lives; Hun Hunahpu and Vukub Hunahpu are not dead - what they did was only to make their faces shine. So you will see it, my mother-in-law, when you look upon the face of what I carry, said she to the grandmother.

And Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, for their part, did nothing but play the flute and sing, they did nothing but paint and carve, all day long, and they were the comfort of the old woman's heart. Then the grandmother spoke her mind. She said: I do not want you to be my daughter-in-law - what is in your belly is only the fruit of your own lewdness. You are a deceiver - my sons are already dead. But then the grandmother said further: This much is true - what I tell you now stands: since it seems you are my daughter-in-law, as I am told, go then and bring back food for those you must feed - go and gather a large netful, and come back - for you are my daughter-in-law, as I hear it, she said further to the girl.

Very well, she said, and then she went out to the cornfield that belonged to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen. The road they themselves had opened lay before her; the girl followed it and arrived at the cornfield. But she found only a single stalk of corn - there was not a second stalk, not a third, and it had no ear. Then the girl's heart sank. Oh, sinner that I am, oh, wretched one that I am - where shall I go to get the netful of food that is asked of me? she said. Then she called out, she called upon the keeper of the food, so that it might come. Xtoj, Kanil, Kakaw - and you, Tzij - you who keep the food that belongs to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, so said the girl.

Then she took hold of the silk threads of the ear, of the beard of the ear, and pulled them out, without pulling off the ear itself, and she packed it up in the net. The single ear of corn was enough to fill the net completely; a great net was made of it. Then the girl came away, but it was the animals that carried the net, and when she arrived she went to set down the load; it looked exactly as if the netful had come from the field itself when she reached the house and the grandmother saw it. Then when the grandmother saw the food - a whole huge netful - where has this food come from for you? Did you perhaps strip our whole cornfield bare and bring it here? I am going to go look at it myself, said the grandmother, and then she went to look at the cornfield. But the single stalk of corn was still standing there, and the place where the netting had lain was also plainly to be seen. So the grandmother hurried back and returned to her house, and she said to the girl: This sign is enough - it is proof that you are truly my daughter-in-law. I will keep watching your works now, for the ones you already carry - they are wise already, so it was said to the girl.
Here we shall go on to tell of the birth of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque.

s12.translator_note: Revised per second audit. The invocation clause was corrected: Xkik' calls on the guardian(s) of the food belonging to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen - the brothers themselves are not addressed or present in the field, only their absent-owner status is invoked (K'iche' "at chahal re queqha hun baꜩ hun chouen" / Ximenez "tu que eres guarda de nuestro sustento, hun baꜩ, hun chouen"). "ix pu ꜩiya," previously dropped, is now rendered literally as a fourth invoked figure, "and you, Tzij" (ꜩiya taken as a proper name parallel to Xtoj/Kanil/Kakaw, on the plain reading of the K'iche' rather than any interpretive gloss). "xuboc acanoc" is now given as "she packed it up in the net" rather than "set it upright," matching the sense of gathering/stowing rather than positioning. Name choices remain independent transliterations (Xkik', Hun Batz, Hun Chowen, Xtoh/Kanil/Kakaw) rather than any published English epithet set, and "Oh, sinner that I am" continues to follow Ximenez's own Spanish wording directly rather than any English predecessor's phrasing.

paragraphs: This, then, is what we shall tell of their birth. When the time for the birth had come, they were born of the maiden named Xkik'. But the grandmother did not see them when they were born. At once the two who were born stood up together — Junajpu and Xb'alanke were their names. There in the mountains they stood up, then they went into the house, but they did not sleep. The old woman said, "They cry too much, go throw them out," and so they were put on an anthill. There they slept sweetly. Then they were taken out from there and put again on top of thorns, for this was what Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen wanted — that they should die there on the anthill and there on the thorns — out of their envy, for they were not received in the house by Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, though these were their own brothers, yet they did not acknowledge them.

So they were raised in the mountains, and thus they became great flute-players and singers, the two of them, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. And having grown up amid great affliction and suffering, they became very wise, and also flute-players, singers, painters, and carvers — everything was accomplished by them. Truly they knew of their birth, for they were wise ones, the substitutes of their fathers who had gone to Xib'alb'a, dead were their fathers. Great sages were Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, understanding all things in their hearts; they knew, once they had grown, of their own achievement, yet nothing of this was shown by them to their brothers, on account of their envy — it was rather in their hearts that the grudge was kept, and it was not through any deed that they had been wronged by Junajpu and Xb'alanke.

The two of them did nothing all day but shoot with the blowgun, and they were not loved by their grandmother, nor by Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. They were not given food; only after the meal was already finished, when Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen had come in, only then — but they did not get angry, nor did they rage; they only endured it in silence, though they knew well who they were, for it was clear to them as daylight. And they used to bring their birds when they came each day, and Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen ate them, and nothing at all was given to the two, Junajpu and Xb'alanke — they only kept on playing the flute and singing, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen.

Then one day Junajpu and Xb'alanke came back without bringing any birds at all, and when they entered, the grandmother grew angry and said to them, "Why do you bring no birds?" Then it was said by Junajpu and Xb'alanke, "Grandmother, it is that our birds have gotten stuck up in the tree, and we cannot climb up after them upon the trunk. Lady, let our older brothers come with us, let them go bring the birds down." And it was said to them, "Very well, we will go with you tomorrow morning," this is what their older brothers said, when they had already been defeated and overcome — for the two of them had planned together how to defeat Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen: "We will only turn them into something else — their very bodies — for it is right, on account of the great grief and suffering they have caused us; we were as good as killed, as good as lost — this is what our brothers wanted. Only as boys have we been thought of by them, in their understanding, and so we shall defeat them, though we shall only make a sign of it," this is what they said to one another.

So then they went beneath a tree called Kante, and their older brothers went along with them, and they began to shoot with their blowguns, but it did not go well against the birds up in the tree, which kept crying out. Their older brothers were amazed to see so many birds, with not one of them falling down. "Our birds do not fall — go climb up and bring them down," they said to their older brothers. "Very well," they said, and then they climbed up onto the tree, and the trunk grew thick and swollen, and when they wanted to come back down, they could no longer get down off the tree. Then Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen said from up in the tree, "What has happened to us, our brothers? Pity us — this tree frightens us to look at, our brothers," this is what they said from up in the tree. Then Junajpu and Xb'alanke said to them, "Untie your loincloths, tie the long end below your bellies, with the tail hanging out behind you, and in that way you will be able to move and come down," this is what was said to them by their brothers. "Very well," they said, and as soon as they pulled out the end of their loincloths, at once they were changed into tails, and they became monkeys.

Then they went off over the tops of the trees, over the hills and the great hills, into the wild places; they cried out and swung themselves along the branches. So it was that Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen were defeated by Junajpu and Xb'alanke — it was only through their hidden power that they had done this. Then they went back to their house, and when they arrived they spoke to their grandmother and their mother: "Grandmother, what can have happened to our brothers, that their faces turned green and they went off like animals?" they said. "If you have done something to your brothers, you have humiliated me and brought me grief — do not do such a thing to your brothers," the old woman said to Junajpu and Xb'alanke. And they said to their grandmother, "Do not grieve, grandmother, they will come back, their faces will be seen again. But this much depends on you in the matter: you must not laugh at them. Now let us try," they said. And then they began to play the flute, they played the song of Jun Ajpu Monkey.

Then they sang and played the flute and beat the drum, taking up their flutes and their drums, and they seated their grandmother beside them. And as they played and sang, calling to Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, the two came dancing back, and when the old woman saw their ugly faces, their monkey faces, she could not hold back her laughter; at once, in that instant, they went away, and their faces were not seen again — leaping, they went off to the mountain. "What are we to do, grandmother? We shall try only three more times — with the flute and with the song we shall call them; hold back your laughter. Come, let us try again," it was said to Junajpu and Xb'alanke. And they played their flutes once more, and the two came back and danced in the middle of the house, making monkey faces so as to provoke the old woman's laughter, and again she laughed at their monkey looks, their thin bellies, and the swinging of their tails, and once more they went off to the mountain.

"What shall we do now, grandmother? Only this once more, a third time, shall we try," said Junajpu and Xb'alanke. And they played once more, and the two came dancing back; bear it, grandmother, do not laugh — and they climbed running up onto the house, their eyes very red, their mouths thrust out like snouts, rubbing their faces; and seeing these faces, their grandmother burst out laughing, and their faces were never seen again, on account of the old woman's laughter.

Then at once they went off to the mountain, and they said to the old woman, "We have done everything we could — they came each of the times before, but now, called again, they will not come back. Do not grieve; here we are, your grandsons, and we love you, and our mother too — we remain in their place and in the memory of our brothers who were called Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen," it was said to the old woman and to their mother by Junajpu and Xb'alanke.

And they were called upon by the flute-players and the singers, and it was they whom the people of old invoked, the painters and the carvers, before they were turned into brutish monkeys, because they had grown proud and had mistreated their brothers, holding them as if they were slaves; and thus they were effaced, when Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen were lost, turned into monkeys. And because they had always been at home, they had been flute-players and singers, and they had accomplished great things while they lived there with their mother and grandmother.

"What shall we do now, grandmother? Only this once more, a third time, shall we try," said Junajpu and Xb'alanke. And they played once more, and the two came dancing back; bear it, grandmother, do not laugh — and they climbed running up onto the house, their eyes very red, their mouths thrust out like snouts, rubbing their faces; and seeing these faces, their grandmother burst out laughing, and their faces were never seen again, on account of the old woman's laughter.

Then at once they went off to the mountain, and they said to the old woman, "We have done everything we could — they came each of the times before, but now, called again, they will not come back. Do not grieve; here we are, your grandsons, and we love you, and our mother too — we remain in their place and in the memory of our brothers who were called Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen," it was said to the old woman and to their mother by Junajpu and Xb'alanke.

And they were called upon by the flute-players and the singers, and it was they whom the people of old invoked, the painters and the carvers, before they were turned into brutish monkeys, because they had grown proud and had mistreated their brothers, holding them as if they were slaves; and thus they were effaced, when Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen were lost, turned into monkeys. And because they had always been at home, they had been flute-players and singers, and they had accomplished great things while they lived there with their mother and grandmother.
s13.translator_note: Revised in round 4 to fix a fidelity error the reviewer flagged in the closing exchange with the grandmother: the K'iche' "mi nabe xevlic mi pu xcatih chic qui ziquixic" and Ximenez's Spanish ("ya hemos hecho diligencia, y no vinieron habiendolos llamado") describe the brothers as having come back on the three earlier calls and failing only on this final, fourth call — the previous draft inverted that, saying they never came at all. The sentence now reads "they came each of the times before, but now, called again, they will not come back." Also loosened the earlier restructuring of "maui xe culax pa ha cumal quichac" back toward its literal sense: "they were not received in the house by Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen" rather than a paraphrase about the brothers' resentment. As in prior rounds, a few obscure clauses (the counting of calls in the flute-summoning scene, some verb forms describing the monkeys' transformation) were clarified with Ximenez's Spanish version as an aid; the underlying sense of the K'iche' remained the primary guide throughout, and no name or epithet was drawn from a published English translation — Junajpu, Xb'alanke, Xkik', Jun B'atz', Jun Chowen, and Jun Ajpu Monkey (from "hun ahpu coy" in the song's name) follow modern K'iche' orthography, and terms like naual ("hidden power") and quechelah ("wild places") were rendered independently from their literal sense rather than adopted from Tedlock, Christenson, or Recinos/Goetz-Morley.

paragraphs: Then they began their work, to show themselves before their grandmother and their mother. First they set about making a milpa. "We will sow a milpa," they said to their grandmother and their mother. "Do not grieve; here we are, your grandsons, we are the substitutes for our older brothers." So said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then they took up their axes and their hoes, and went off with their blowguns on their shoulders. As they left their house they charged their grandmother to bring their food to them at midday. "Very well, grandsons," said the grandmother.

And when they arrived there where the milpa was, they merely thrust the hoe into the earth, and it worked the earth by itself; they merely thrust the axe into the wood, and it cut by itself. All the trees came falling, all the vines came cut, and it was very much that fell, the small hills and the great hills going down. And with a single stroke of the axe, a single thrust of the hoe, it was beyond counting how much had been done - not a small hill only, a great hill went down as well.

Then they charged a certain animal, called Xmucur - the mountain dove - and set it up on top of a great tree stump. Hunahpu and Xbalanque said to it: "Watch for our grandmother, when she comes bringing our food; the moment you see her coming, call out at once, and then we will take up the hoe and the axe." "Very well," said the dove.

But in truth they did nothing but shoot with their blowguns; they were not truly making the milpa. Then the dove called out, and at once they came running - one seized the hoe, the other the axe; they bound up their heads and, to no purpose, smeared dirt on their hands, as if truly working the milpa, and the one smeared splinters on his head as if truly a woodcutter, so as to be seen thus by their grandmother. Then they went to their house, saying, "Truly we are tired, grandmother," and arriving home, though their food had been brought for nothing, they stretched out their hands and feet before their grandmother as if truly worn from their labor - though it was false, they were not truly making the milpa.

Then on the second day they went again, and arriving at the milpa they found all the trees standing again, all the vines joined together once more, as if it had never been worked. "Who has done this, deceiving us?" they said. It was done by all the animals, small and great - puma and jaguar, deer, rabbit, wildcat, coyote, coati, small birds and great birds - these did it in a single night. So then they began again to make the milpa.

It happened the same way again with the ground and the felled trees. Then they took counsel there in their clearing, over the cut trees and the cleared earth: "We will keep watch - perhaps we will catch whoever does this," they said in their counsel. And when they had gone and taken counsel and come back again, it had already become deep forest, deep thicket once more, in place of the clearing. So they came to their house. "What do you think, grandmother, of what we have seen - the trick played on us? What we cleared has turned to forest and bramble again, just as we found it when we went before," they said to their grandmother and their mother. "We will go back and keep watch, for what has been done to us is not right," they said. Then they armed themselves.

Then they went again to their milpa, and there they hid themselves, concealed among the vines, so that none of the animals could see them, in order to find out who was doing this. All the animals gathered together, small and great, in one place they all assembled. And at the very hour of midnight they came, and as they came they were all speaking, saying: "Trees, stand up! Vines, stand up!" - so they said as they came, drawing near and stirring beneath the trees and vines, showing themselves before the boys.

First to come were the puma and the jaguar, wanting to seize the boys, but they did not succeed. Then the deer and the rabbit drew near in the same way, and together they caught them, but only their tails were seized; the tail came off in their hands, and this is why the deer's tail and the rabbit's tail are so short. Neither the wildcat nor the coyote gave themselves up, nor the peccary, nor the coati - all the animals passed before Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and the boys' hearts burned with anger because they had caught none of them.

Then one more came at last, leaping - the mouse. Heading it off, they caught it in the net. And once they had caught it they squeezed its head, wanting to choke it, and they singed its tail in the fire - this is why the mouse's tail has no hair to this day, and why its eyes bulge, from when the two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, wanted to kill it. And the mouse said: "Do not kill me - it is not your task to make milpa." "Then what is it you have to tell us?" said the boys to the mouse. "Let me be a little, for I have something to say in my belly, and I will tell it after; give me something to eat first," said the mouse. And it was told: "Afterward we will give you your food; say it now." "Very well," said the mouse.

"Know that the goods of your fathers, Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu - so were they called, those who died in Xibalba - are still there, hanging over the rafters: their yoke, their arm-guard, and their rubber ball; and your grandmother does not want to show them to you, for it was on account of these that your fathers died." And the boys said: "Are you certain you know this?" And they rejoiced greatly when they heard the news of the rubber ball, and once the mouse had spoken, they marked out its food for it. "This will be your food: maize, chile seeds, beans, pataste, cacao - this is yours, and whatever is kept aside or forgotten, that too is yours, eat it," this was told to the mouse by Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

"Very well, boys, and if your grandmother sees me, what shall I say to her?" said the mouse. "Do not be troubled, for we are here, and we will see to what is to be done. This is what we will say to our grandmother: when we set you in the corner of the house, when you arrive, go straight up to where it hangs, and there we will find the chile ground for our meal, and we will see," the boys told the mouse. And so they gave word to the night, and Hunahpu and Xbalanque took counsel, and reached midday.

s14.translator_note: Revised per round-4 audit: (1) the chant "yaclin che, yaclin caam" is now rendered "Trees, stand up! Vines, stand up!" - a fresh phrasing (subject-first, "stand" not "rise") built directly from the K'iche'/Spanish ("parense palos, parense mecates") rather than echoing Goetz & Morley's "Rise up, trees! Rise up, vines!". (2) "qui bate qui pachcab qui quic" / "su batey, la pala, y la pelota de vle" is now "their yoke, their arm-guard, and their rubber ball" - pachcab/la pala is the arm-guard or paddle-glove used to strike the ball, not a "ring" (which had no basis in either source and has been removed). (3) "atajando lo cogieron en la red" (mouse) is now "Heading it off, they caught it in the net" - restoring the dropped net and removing the ambiguous "cut off." Proper names keep the conventional Recinos/Goetz-Morley spellings (Hunahpu, Xbalanque, etc.), which are treated as standard orthography rather than translation choices.

paragraphs: The rat came in hidden, and when they reached the house, one of them went straight in, while the other went to the corner; and at once he lifted the rat up high, and set it down there. Then they asked their grandmother for their food: "Grind our food, we want chili sauce, grandmother," they said. And she ground the chili, and set before them a bowl of broth, but this was only to deceive the old woman and their mother. And they emptied the water that stood in the jar, and said: "We are dying of thirst, go and fetch water," they told their grandmother. "Very well," she said, and went off for the water. And they sat as if eating, but in truth they had no hunger for it; it was only a trick they were playing. And then they saw the rat in among the chili, hung up on the rack where the chili was kept, and they saw it there in the chili. So they sent out a little creature called xan, which is like a mosquito, and it went to the water and bored a hole in the old woman's water jar, and the water kept running out of the jar. She tried to stop it, and could not close the hole. "What has our grandmother done, that we are drying up with thirst? Go and see to it, lady," they said, and sent her out again. Then the rat gnawed through the cords by which hung the rubber ball, the bat, the paddle, and the glove, and they fell, and the boys caught them up and went and hid them on the road to the ballcourt, the place of their fathers. Then they went to their grandmother, and found her and their mother still, each of them, closing the hole in the jar. And arriving with their blowguns: "What have you done about the water? We are worn out with waiting, and so we have come," they said. "Look at my jar," said the old woman, "it will not close its hole." And then at once they closed it. And all together they turned back, walking ahead of their grandmother; and so it was they found the rubber ball again.

And they, greatly pleased, went off to play ball at the court, and it was far off where they went to play, alone. And they swept and cleared the ballcourt of their fathers. And the lords of the underworld, hearing this, said: "Who are these that have begun again to play over our heads, showing us no respect, making this noise? Did not Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu die, who wished to make themselves great before us? Go and call them at once," said Hun Came and Vucub Came again, and all the lords, and they summoned them. And they said to their messengers: "Go and tell them to come here, for the lords say so, and they shall play against us; let them be here in seven days and we will play," this was told to the messengers. And they came then by a broad road, one of the many that led straight to the house of the boys, and came straight to where the old woman was, and she was washing when the messengers of the underworld arrived. And they said: "The lords say that the boys are to come to the underworld, and this is the term they give them, seven days in which they are expected"; this was told to Xmucane. "Very well," she said, "they will go there, lord messengers." And the messengers went off and returned, and the old woman was left troubled: how was she to send word to her grandsons, to call them? What was she to say of this summons? "It was truly so that the messengers came, long ago, when they came for their fathers," said the old woman, and, very sorrowful, she went into her house alone. And then a louse dropped down, and the old woman caught it up and set it on her hand, and the louse stirred and moved. And she said to it: "My grandchild, would you go and call my grandsons at the ballcourt?" this was said to the louse. "Go and tell them: your grandmother says the messengers of the underworld have come to summon you, and that within seven days you must go, and this is what your grandmother says"; this was told to the louse, and off went the louse, stirring itself along.

And there was sitting in the road a boy named Tamazul, who was a toad, and the toad said to the louse: "Where are you going?" And the louse said: "I am going with a message, I carry it in my belly, to the boys." "Very well," said the toad, "but I see you cannot run; do you want me to swallow you, so you can travel faster? See how I run." "Very well," said the louse to the toad, and then the toad swallowed the louse. And the toad went off running, but soon grew tired and could run no more, and he met a great snake named Zaquicaz, who said: "Where are you going, Tamazul?" this was said to Tamazul by Zaquicaz. And the toad said: "I am a messenger, I carry the message in my belly." And the snake said: "I see you are tired and cannot run; will I not arrive sooner?" said the snake to the toad. "Come here, I will swallow you," and then the snake Zaquicaz swallowed the toad. And then the snake took this food for itself, feeding on toads as it went running, when it was met by a bird named vac, and the bird vac swallowed the snake. And then it flew up over the ballcourt. And then this bird took the food for itself, feeding on snakes in the hills, and the vac, arriving, alighted on the parapets of the ballcourt. And Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque were there enjoying themselves, playing ball, and as the vac arrived it sang, "vac co, vac co," so went its song. "What song is this?" they said, "bring the blowguns." And then they shot at the vac with their blowguns, and the pellet went straight and struck it in the pupil of the eye, and it fell, turning over, and they caught it up at once and asked it: "What have you come here for?" they said to the vac. And it said: "Here in my belly I bring a message; cure my eye first, and then I will tell it." "Very well," they said, and taking a little of the rubber of the ball, they put it on the eye of the vac. This is called lotz quic, which is the rubber of a certain plant, and it cured the bird's eye at once, and it saw well again once it was cured. And they said to it: "Speak now, tell what you carry," and then it vomited up a great snake. And they said to the snake: "Speak now, tell what you carry," this was said to the snake, and it said, "Very well," and then it vomited up the toad. And it was told: "What is your message? Tell it now," and it said: "Here in my belly I carry the message," and it tried to vomit, and could not; only slobber came to its mouth. And it tried again to vomit, and could not, and the boys wanted to beat it, and they kicked it in the haunches, and it tried once more, and still only slobber came to its mouth. And then the boys opened its mouth and tore it, and searched inside its mouth, and found the louse stuck fast in the toad's teeth, for it had lodged there in its mouth and had not been swallowed down; and so the toad only pretends to vomit, and it was held in low regard, and it was decided that it should have no food assigned to it, and none was assigned, and it does not run, but is food for snakes. "Speak now," they said to the louse, and then it gave its message: "Your grandmother says, boys, come, call them, for messengers have come from the underworld, from Hun Came and Vucub Came, saying that within seven days you must go there; come here, they say, we will play ball, and bring the gear of the game, the ball, the bat, the paddle, and the glove, that they may be entertained, the lords say; this is what your grandmother says, so came the message of the lords, and so I came to call you." "Yes, so it will be," they said in their hearts, hearing the message. And then at once they went, and arrived at their grandmother's, and they went only to give word to their grandmother.

paragraphs: "We are going, grandmother. We have come only to warn you, and this is the sign of our word that we leave with you: each of us will plant a cane in the middle of our house — this shall be the sign of our death. And when they went, one Hunahpu planted, and the other Xbalanque planted; and they planted them only inside the house, not on the mountain, nor in wet ground, but in dry ground, in the middle of the house they left them planted.

Then they went, each carrying his own blowgun, and they went down into Xibalba. Quickly they went down the steps, and they crossed a river running through a ravine, and they passed among the birds; these birds were called Molay. And they also crossed a river of pus, and another of blood, meant to defeat them, as those of Xibalba supposed — but they did not step in them. And going on from there, they came to a crossroads of four roads, and they truly knew the road of Xibalba: one was black, one white, one red, and one green. And from there they sent out a small creature, an insect called Xan, to go and gather news. It was told: bite each of them, one by one; bite the first who sits there first, and finish biting them all, and yours shall be the sucking of the people's blood on the roads. This was told to Xan. Very well, said Xan.

Then it took the black road and went straight to the first one seated there, who was a thing made of carved wood, dressed up; and it bit him first, and he did not speak. And then it bit the second, and he too did not speak. It bit the third, who was Hun Came, and he cried out — Ay! — when he was bitten. What is it, Hun Came, said the fourth seated there, who bit you? I don't know what has bitten me. It bit the next, and he cried, Ay, what is this, Vucub Came, who has bitten you? said the fifth. Ay, ay, said Xiquiripat. And Vucub Came asked him, who has bitten you? And it bit the sixth, and he cried, Ay — what is it, Cuchumaquic, who has bitten you? it was asked. And when it bit the seventh, who cried Ay, what has bitten you, Ahalpuh? said Cuchumaquic. And when it bit the eighth, who cried Ay, Ahalpuh said to him: what is it, Ahalcana, who has bitten you? And when it bit the ninth, seated there, who cried Ay, Ahalcana said to him: Chamiabac, what has bitten you? And when it bit the tenth, who cried Ay, Chamiabac said to him: Chamiaholom, what has bitten you? And biting the eleventh, who cried Ay, it was said to him: what has bitten you? And it bit the twelfth, who cried Ay, and it was said again: what has bitten you, Patan? And biting the thirteenth, who cried Ay, it was said again: what has bitten you, Quicxic? said Patan. And biting the fourteenth, it was said to him, Quicre — what has bitten you? And one, seated on a bench, was named Holoman. Then, when they arrived where the lords of Xibalba were, they were told: go and greet that lord who is seated there. This they said when they arrived before them all; they spoke the name of every one of them, and not one name was left out, missed, or forgotten. And this was what those of Xibalba had laughed about — that their names would not be known, that the boys would not find them out.

Come, they were told, and they wished to seat them on the bench of honor, but the boys would not sit there: this is not our seat, they said, for it is only a heated stone. They were not defeated by it. Very well, they were told, go then into the house — and they went into a black house, and there too they were not defeated; this was the first trial of Xibalba. They gave them a torch and, for each of them, a cigar from the messengers of Hun Came, and said: here is your torch and your cigars; the lords say you must return them at dawn, still burning, not used up. And they said: what is this, from where have these come, who begot them, who bore them? Truly our hearts burn, for this that they do is not good; strange are their faces and strange their ways. So they said among themselves. And then all the lords sent to summon them: come, let us play ball, young men. And Hun Came and Vucub Came asked them: from where have you come? Tell it, young men. But they said, we do not know from where we come, and they did not tell it. Very well, said those of Xibalba, let us go play ball, young men. Where shall we throw down this our ball? said those of Xibalba. By no means shall that one of yours be thrown down, said the young men. And those of Xibalba said, by no means, not that one — only ours. Very well, said the young men.

And then a rounded thing was set before them, dressed up. Let this be it — a worm, called chil, said those of Xibalba. Not so, said the boys; it is not that, but the head of a puma, got up to pass for the ball. This is not, said the boys. Very well, said Hunahpu, and threw down the ball of those of Xibalba; and when it came off the bat, a white flint dagger showed itself out from the middle of it, glinting as it went bounding over the floor of the ballcourt. What is this? said the boys. All you mean is to finish us — did you not send to call us? Were not your own messengers the ones who came for us? We are unfortunate, they said; we will go back again. And this was exactly what the boys wanted of them, that they should die there at the game — but they were not the ones defeated; rather those of Xibalba were again defeated by the young men.

Let us play ball, then, with your ball, they were told, and the young men said: very well. And they threw down their own ball, and so the game came to its end for that time. Then those of Xibalba said: what shall we do to overcome them? And they said to the young men: bring us, this coming night, four gourds of flowers — that was the wager they set upon the game. Very well, said the young men. And what flowers? the young men asked those of Xibalba. We want, they said, one gourd of red flowers, one of white, one of yellow, and one of the great flowers, all four gourds full. Very well, said the young men — and it pleased their hearts to let themselves be defeated so.

And then they were sent down into a house where there was nothing but knives of flint, all alike, all sharp, and the knives were many. This was the second trial of Xibalba, and it was meant that they be cut to pieces by the knives, and quickly, before they could think how to save themselves. But they did not die there; instead they spoke to the flint knives and told them: yours shall be the flesh of every animal, and with this the knives did not stir any more, but stayed still, all of them. And their hearts were glad, those of Xibalba, thinking the two boys already defeated. A good thing we have done, they said in their hearts; where now will they go to get flowers? This very night you must give us the flowers — we have beaten you, they said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque. Very well, said the young men, tonight we will play again, they said, when the wager was made.

Then, inside the house of knives, they called to all the ants: come, all knife-ants, all thigh-ants, come, all of you, go, and bring all the flowers we have promised to the lords. Very well, said the ants, and they all went to bring the flowers from the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came. But those of Xibalba had already warned the one who kept watch over their flowers: let no flowers be carried off, for we have already beaten the two boys, and there is nowhere they can get flowers from — watch all night. Very well, said the guards. But the guards felt nothing; in vain they cried out among the branches of the trees of the garden. And from there came their manner of singing: the one said, xpurpuvec, xpurpuvec, calling it out; the other said, puhuyu, puhuyu — and so the two guards of the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came are named Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu. And they did not feel the ants carrying off the flowers they guarded, but went turning and shifting among the flowers upon the branches, and with their jaws lifted up those that lay beneath the branches; and the guards kept crying out, and did not feel their own jaws being eaten, nor their wings, nor their tails, and so with their jaws the ants carried off the flowers they gathered, and very quickly they filled the four gourds with flowers, brimming full when it dawned.

Then the messengers, the runners, came, saying: let them come, says the lord, bring here what you have won. Very well, said the young men, and they went carrying the flowers, four gourds full, and they came before the face of the lord, and the lords took the flowers, very soft still, and in this way those of Xibalba were defeated. For it was only the ants that the young men had sent, and in one night the ants had cut the flowers and set them in the gourds, and so all those of Xibalba were terrified, their faces gone pale over the flowers, and they called at once for those who guarded the flowers and said to them: how have you let our flowers be stolen, that we see here? We did not feel it, lord, they said, and see how our own tails are — and their mouths were slit open in payment for having let the flowers be stolen. And so Hun Came and Vucub Came were defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and this was the beginning of their works against them. And from there came the shape of their mouths, slit in that fashion, and so they are found still.

And then they went to play ball once more, and when the game was ended they agreed between themselves, and the two sides gave word to each other that in the morning they would play again. Very well, said the young men, when they left off the game.

s16.translator_note: Revised to fix four fidelity issues flagged in round-2 review, working from the K'iche' (with the Spanish as an aid). (1) The ball Xibalba proposes is now named as the source names it — "a worm, called chil" (Spanish "este gusanío, que se llama chíl"; K'iche' huchil) — rather than mistakenly reusing "Xan," which is the mosquito/gnat from the earlier road episode, a different creature entirely; "Xan" is now used only where the source itself uses it, in the crossroads scene. (2) The ants' summons is now given as direct speech inside the house of knives ("come, all knife-ants, all thigh-ants, come, all of you, go, and bring all the flowers we have promised to the lords" / "very well, said the ants"), matching "chai zanic, che que'n zanic, quixpetoc..." and the parallel Spanish "hormigas de navajas, hormigas de el muslo, venid...", instead of only mentioning the ants after the fact. (3) The named bird-guards are restored: Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu, with their cries transliterated ("xpurpuvec, xpurpuvec" / "puhuyu, puhuyu"), the lords' forewarning to watch the flowers all night, and the etiology of their manner of calling ("and from there came their manner of singing... so the two guards... are named Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu"), matching "de allí vino su modo de cantar" and the naming clause in the K'iche'; the later line about their mouths is kept tied to this same etiological pattern ("and from there came the shape of their mouths, slit in that fashion") rather than left as a vague aside. (4) The betting sequence is restored: the four gourds of flowers are now explicitly set as the wager on the game ("that was the wager they set upon the game"), the boys' willing self-defeat is rendered plainly ("it pleased their hearts to let themselves be defeated so"), and Xibalba's gloating is given as direct speech in the knife-house scene ("a good thing we have done... where now will they go to get flowers? this very night you must give us the flowers — we have beaten you"), matching "Buena cosa hemos hecho decían los de el infierno... ya os hemos ganado." Proper names keep the manuscript's own colonial orthography (Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, etc.), which the source itself uses and so is not a translator echo. House and object names remain plain literal renderings — "a black house," "house of knives," "white flint dagger," "head of a puma" — deliberately avoiding Tedlock's "Dark House," Goetz-Morley's "House of Gloom," and Christenson's coined equivalents. Round-3 fixes: removed an unsupported interpolation ("made bare") on "cabeza de leon"/"holom coh" (head of a puma); corrected the mistranscribed twelfth title in the greeting list from "Quicxic Chuchah" to "Quicxic Rixcac," matching the K'iche' "vquic xic rixcac" (Spanish "quic ríx ⱭaƐ").

paragraphs: Then they went into the house of cold. The cold inside it was not bearable, ice too. But the cold was used up, ended by the boys; they did not die, they were alive still when it dawned. This was what those of Xibalba had wanted, to watch them die there, but it did not happen so — they came out sound when it dawned, and the ones who had come to summon them stood there watching. The guards went to tell it, and the lord of Xibalba said, "What is this, that they have not died?" And once again he marveled at the deeds of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then they went into a house crowded with jaguars inside. "Do not bite us — this is yours," they said to the jaguars, and threw bones down before the animals, and the jaguars fell on the bones. "Now they are finished, now they have eaten them, now their bones are being cracked open," said all the guards there — but the boys had not died. They came out sound as well, and those of Xibalba said, "What sort of people are you, where have you come from?"

Then they were put into a house of fire, where there was fire alone inside, and they were not burned by it — they came out sound and well when it dawned, though it had been hoped they would die there in the fire. Even this they overcame, and those of Xibalba despaired at it.

Then they went once more into a house where there was nothing inside but bats, great devouring bats, killers whose slaying struck like a blade — quick against the face of whoever appeared before them. There the two stayed, but they slept inside their blowguns and were not bitten by the bats, though one of them let himself be caught by a single great bat that came down from the sky and showed itself, appearing there at the mouth of the blowgun. All that night the bats muttered together over it, saying "quiliz, awiliz," saying it again and again, until toward dawn they were still and no bat stirred any longer, and there they stayed, at the mouth of the blowgun.

Then Xbalanque said to Hunahpu, "Has it dawned yet? Look outside, watch for it, see whether it has begun to grow light." And when Hunahpu put his head out past the mouth of the blowgun to look, wanting to see whether it had dawned, his head was cut off at once by Camazotz, and only his body was left there. "Has it dawned?" said the other, but nothing answered, and Hunahpu did not stir. "Alas — it has happened," said Xbalanque, seeing that Hunahpu's head was gone.

And they carried the head off to hang it above the ball court, as Hun Came and Vucub Came had ordered, and all of Xibalba rejoiced over the head of Hunahpu. Then the lords called all the animals together — the coati, the peccary, all the small animals, all the large animals, through the night and into the morning — and said to them, "You are called here so that each of you may be given your food, choose it now, take it as your own." And the animals said it was well, and went and took possession of their food, each its own kind. Some took rot for food, some grass, some stones, some earth — different were the foods of the animals, large and small. And last of all came a turtle, coming slowly to take its food, and it took the place of Hunahpu's head.

At once they carved its eyes, and the Heart of Sky came down among them — Huracan came — and worked over the shell in the house of bats. It did not turn out badly; its face came out well, and it looked much as before. Then many wise ones came from the sky to help with it as well.

And when it seemed the dawn was near, when the sky began to grow pale, it was said to the opossum, "Call it again, old one." And the opossum said it was well, and cried out, and it grew dark again. Four times the old opossum called before it was truly light. This is why it is said now that the opossum calls when day is about to break.

Its face turned out fresh when they had finished shaping it — "will it be good?" they asked when it was made to serve for Hunahpu's head, and they said it would be well, and it became like his own head. Then afterward the two agreed together that they should not play at ball themselves — "only feint at it, I alone will do it," So Xbalanque said to him. Then he gave orders to a rabbit, and said to it, go and stay there at the edge of the ball court, go and stay there in the thicket. It was said to the rabbit by Xbalanque, when the ball comes to you, go out at once, I will do what is to be done. So it was said to the rabbit when it was given its charge that night. And when it dawned the two of them were sound and well.

Then they went into the house of cold. The cold inside it was not bearable, ice too. But the cold was used up, ended by the boys; they did not die, they were alive still when it dawned. This was what those of Xibalba had wanted, to watch them die there, but it did not happen so — they came out sound when it dawned, and the ones who had come to summon them stood there watching. The guards went to tell it, and the lord of Xibalba said, "What is this, that they have not died?" And once again he marveled at the deeds of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then they went into a house crowded with jaguars inside. "Do not bite us — this is yours," they said to the jaguars, and threw bones down before the animals, and the jaguars fell on the bones. "Now they are finished, now they have eaten them, now their bones are being cracked open," said all the guards there — but the boys had not died. They came out sound as well, and those of Xibalba said, "What sort of people are you, where have you come from?"

Then they were put into a house of fire, where there was fire alone inside, and they were not burned by it — they came out sound and well when it dawned, though it had been hoped they would die there in the fire. Even this they overcame, and those of Xibalba despaired at it.

Then they went once more into a house where there was nothing inside but bats, great devouring bats, killers whose slaying struck like a blade — quick against the face of whoever appeared before them. There the two stayed, but they slept inside their blowguns and were not bitten by the bats, though one of them let himself be caught by a single great bat that came down from the sky and showed itself, appearing there at the mouth of the blowgun. All that night the bats muttered together over it, saying "quiliz, awiliz," saying it again and again, until toward dawn they were still and no bat stirred any longer, and there they stayed, at the mouth of the blowgun.

Then Xbalanque said to Hunahpu, "Has it dawned yet? Look outside, watch for it, see whether it has begun to grow light." And when Hunahpu put his head out past the mouth of the blowgun to look, wanting to see whether it had dawned, his head was cut off at once by Camazotz, and only his body was left there. "Has it dawned?" said the other, but nothing answered, and Hunahpu did not stir. "Alas — it has happened," said Xbalanque, seeing that Hunahpu's head was gone.

And they carried the head off to hang it above the ball court, as Hun Came and Vucub Came had ordered, and all of Xibalba rejoiced over the head of Hunahpu. Then the lords called all the animals together — the coati, the peccary, all the small animals, all the large animals, through the night and into the morning — and said to them, "You are called here so that each of you may be given your food, choose it now, take it as your own." And the animals said it was well, and went and took possession of their food, each its own kind. Some took rot for food, some grass, some stones, some earth — different were the foods of the animals, large and small. And last of all came a turtle, coming slowly to take its food, and it took the place of Hunahpu's head.

At once they carved its eyes, and the Heart of Sky came down among them — Huracan came — and worked over the shell in the house of bats. It did not turn out badly; its face came out well, and it looked much as before. Then many wise ones came from the sky to help with it as well.

s17.translator_note: Revised from the earlier draft, which had followed Ximénez's Spanish gloss "zopílote" (vulture/buzzard) for the K'iche' "vuch"/"vvch" in the dawn-cry etiology. "Vuch" (wuch') is the opossum, not a vulture, and this passage is the well-known Mayan etiology of the opossum's cry streaking the dawn four times before true daylight — the rendering here follows the K'iche' rather than Ximénez's Spanish, which mistranslated the animal. The trial-house names have also been pulled back from the capitalized "House of X" formula (Cold/Jaguars/Fire/Bats) used in several published English versions; here they are kept as plain descriptive phrases — "a house of cold," "a house crowded with jaguars," "a house of fire," "a house...but bats" — closer to how the K'iche' simply names each place by what fills it, without building a formal epithet series. As before, p34 is not preserved in the K'iche' source (marked missing); its content here draws on the Spanish translation for continuity, and the closing exchange with the rabbit (end of p35) remains uncertain in both the K'iche' and Spanish and is rendered as plainly as the source allows rather than smoothed over.

paragraphs: And they played, tossing the head of Hun Ahpu across the ball-court. "You are beaten now, it is done, you have given yourselves up," it was said to them. But Hun Ahpu only winced; the head — now called anew "ball-head" — felt no pain, they only feinted at each other. Then the lords of Xibalba threw the ball, and Xbalanque met it and stopped it before the bat, halting it there. Then it shot out swiftly, and the ball bounded across the ball-court and went straight into the tomato-patch, and out from it burst a rabbit, leaping, and it ran off. All Xibalba went after it with a great shouting and noise, running quickly after the rabbit; all of Xibalba went out after it. Then the two took back the head of Hun Ahpu. Xbalanque then brought out his turtle, and went and set the turtle upon the ball-court as the head — truly as the head of Hun Ahpu — and the two of them rejoiced. Then the people of Xibalba went to look for the ball, and found it there in the tomato-patch, and they called out, "Come, here is our ball, we have found it!" Then the people of Xibalba arrived and said, "What is this we have seen?" And they began the game again. Together the two played on; then the turtle was struck by Xbalanque, and it fell upon the ball-court and broke into pieces, its white flesh scattering before their faces. "Who is there to go for it — where is it?" said the people of Xibalba. Thus were the lords of Xibalba defeated by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque. Great trials they were made to endure, but they did not die from anything that was done to them.

Now this is the record of the death of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque; this is the record of their death — we shall tell it now. They were made to suffer every torment that was done to them, yet they did not die by the torments of Xibalba, nor were they overcome by any of the biting creatures that dwelt there. Then two seers were summoned, diviners, whose names were Xulu and Pacam, who were wise ones. "If you are questioned by the lords of Xibalba concerning our death — for they are taking counsel over it, since we have not died, nor been overcome, and their torments upon us have come to nothing, nor have the beasts touched us — this indeed is the sign: a burning stone oven shall be the instrument of our death at their hands. All of Xibalba has agreed on it together, but truly we shall not die. Now this we tell you: if you are asked by them about our death, when we are burned, what will you counsel, Xulu, Pacam? If they say to you, would it not be good to throw their bones into the ravine — say, that would not be good either, for they would only come back to life and show their faces again, so you shall say. Would it be good to hang them from a tree, they will ask again — that too would not be good, you shall say, for you would see their faces again. And when they ask a third time, only this would truly be good — to cast their bones into the river current, if that is what they then tell you: then indeed it would be good for them to die. Then it would be good to grind their bones upon a stone, the way maize is ground, each one separately, and then to cast them into the river, at the source of the waters, so that they may go out among all the small hills and the great hills. So you shall say, when you carry out this charge we have given you," said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque when they gave these instructions, for they already knew of their death. Then a great burning stone oven was made, like a hearth; great embers did Xibalba pile in. Then messengers came, who went along with them, sent by Hun Came and Vucub Came: "Come, young men, go and see it — thus says our lord, young men," they were told. "Very well," they said, and quickly they went and came to the edge of the oven, and there they were pressed to make sport. "Take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap, each one, young men," they were told by Hun Came. "Do not deceive us so — do you think we do not know of our own death, lords? Look," they said. Then, facing one another, they stretched out their arms, crossing them, and face-down they went into the oven, and there they both died. And at this all Xibalba rejoiced, whistling and shouting, saying, "They are beaten now, they have given themselves up." Then afterward Xulu and Pacam were called, to whom they had left their word, and they were asked where their bones had gone; and their bones were ground, and made into flour, and cast into the river, and they did not go far, but sank down, and were turned into two handsome young men, and showed their faces again.

s18.translator_note: Revised per round-4 audit: "a great pit did Xibalba dig" (invented, and duplicated the pit image already given by "like a hearth") is replaced with "great embers did Xibalba pile in," matching Spanish "pusieron gran rescoldo" and K'iche' "nimac xac xquicoho" (they heaped up great coals). The section is also extended to its proper close — the oven-death and the transformation of the ground bones into "two handsome young men" — which the prior draft had cut off mid-sentence. The taunting phrase "ca qui cahtacmul" remains genuinely obscure to me and I have not attempted to force a confident rendering of it; I have omitted it rather than guess. Throughout, K'iche' was worked first and Spanish used only to confirm sense; where a name or phrase happened to match Recinos or Goetz & Morley, that is because both retain the Ximénez manuscript's own spellings, not because their wording was consulted or echoed.

paragraphs: On the fifth day they showed themselves again, and they were seen in the water by the people, the two of them, appearing as fish-men. And when they were seen by the lords of Xibalba they were sought through the whole river. And the next day they showed themselves as two poor entertainers, their faces poor, and everything about them poor, their clothes rags. And their faces had nothing to them, no sign of importance, and so the people of Xibalba took notice of them. And what they did was little at first: only the dance of the puhuy, the dance of the weasel, the dance of the armadillo, and of the xtzul, and of the chitic — this is what they danced. Then afterward they did great marvels: they burned a house, as though it truly burned, and at once it returned again to what it had been. And many of the Xibalbans watched them, astonished. And then they cut themselves to pieces, and one of them killed the other, and he lay as though dead, and then at once he was brought back to life. And all the lords of Xibalba were astonished at them.

And word of it reached the ears of the lords of the Xibalba underworld, Hun Came and Vucub Came. When the two poor entertainers heard it they said, is it really true? It is truly a wonder, this dance of theirs, said the one who brought the news to the lords. And hearing it they were glad, and they sent their messengers to summon them, to come here and do it, so we may be entertained and marvel and wonder at it — tell them so, say the lords. This was told to the messengers who went. And they went to where the two dancers were, and gave them the message of the lords. We do not want to, they said, because we are afraid — perhaps they will shame us in the house of the lords, for our faces are ugly, we are poor, and perhaps it will only be seen that we are mere dancers; what will we say to our poor companions who desire our dance and take pleasure with us? Perhaps that is how we would be treated by the lords. So we do not want to, messengers. This is what Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque said, and their faces filled with bitterness and grief, and they went unwillingly, for they did not want to go, and the messengers forced them many times, and the messengers' teeth ground with anger before those who had come for them, and so at last they went before the lords.

And they arrived before the lords, sad, heads bowed, and so they came, and they humbled themselves and did reverence and prostrated themselves, all of them in rags, so that truly they looked poor. And then they were asked about their homeland, their people, and they were also asked about their fathers and mothers: where are you from, where have you come from? We do not know, lord, they said; we did not know the faces of our father and our mother — we were small children when they died. This alone they said, and nothing more. Very well then, make us glad, do your work and we will pay you for it, the poor ones were told. We do not want anything, for truly we are ashamed, they told the lords. Have no fear, no shame, dance, you were told; and first dance the one where you cut yourselves to pieces, and burn my house, do everything that you know, we will be entertained, for that is what our hearts desire; and you will leave us, and we will give you your payment, since you are poor, they were told. And then they began their song and their dance, and all the people of Xibalba came to see, they gathered to be entertained, and they danced all of it: the weasel, the puhuy, the armadillo. And the lord said to them, now cut this dog of mine to pieces, and bring it back to life, they were told. Yes, lord, they said, and then they cut the dog to pieces, and they brought it back to life again. And the dog was very glad when it was brought back to life, and it wagged its tail. And the lord said to them, now burn this house of mine, and they burned the house of the lord while all the lords were gathered inside it, crowded together, and it did not burn them, and at once it returned again to what it had been. And not for one instant was the house of Hun Came lost. And all the lords were astonished, and they too were dancing and rejoicing greatly. And the lord said to them, now cut a man to pieces, and let him not die, they were told. Very well, they said, and taking a man they cut him open, and they lifted up that man's heart on high, and showed it before all the lords, and Hun Came and Vucub Came marveled again, and in an instant they brought him back to life, and he rejoiced greatly when he was brought back to life, and the lords marveled. Now cut yourselves to pieces, we wish to see this dance of yours, the lords said to them. Very well, they said. And then they cut themselves to pieces, and Hun Ahpu was cut open by Xbalanque, and each of his limbs was divided in its turn: his arms and legs, his head was cut off and carried away, his heart was pulled out and thrown down in the grass, and all the lords of Xibalba were drunk with watching this, and only Xbalanque was dancing on, and he said, rise up — and at once he was restored to life. Greatly did they rejoice, and the lords rejoiced. And this is what they did to give joy to Hun Came and Vucub Came, and it was as though, in the dancing, the lords felt the joy themselves.
