s29.translator_note: Revised per round-1 audit: (1) fixed the final scouting passage, which had inverted the sense — the peoples rejoiced because the defenders they glimpsed were few (maui e harub xeqha / "no eran muchos los que vieron"), while the attacking peoples themselves were vast and their fighting men beyond counting (y los pueblos eran muchos... no eran contables); the spies' report "they are not many" (maui e harub xeqha) is now attributed to what the defenders' side looked like, not the attackers'. (2) Corrected "eyebrows" to "beards": K'iche' quizmachi / Sp. "repelados sus barbas" refers to facial hair, not eyebrows; the eyes are already covered by the preceding clause on their sight being deceived. (3) Fixed "the silver that had gone off to be lost" to "the silver they had stolen ... along the road," per Sp. "que fueron a hurtar al camino" — the dummies were dressed in silver the K'iche' heroes had themselves stolen from the enemy on the road, not silver that had simply vanished. Proper names are kept in the normalized forms used throughout this edition (Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam, Xtah, Xpuch, Tohil, Hacavitz), not Ximénez's manuscript orthography (correcting an earlier note that misdescribed this).

paragraphs: There Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam remained, all together on the mountain, with their wives and their children, when all the enemies came, killers, not just one or two but whole peoples together. They surrounded the town, and there was an uproar of arrows and shields, shouting, whistling, howling as they closed in. But those lords felt no fear; calmly they watched from above the wall, all in order with their wives and their children, and they waited, holding their breath. The peoples below were glad as they climbed the mountain, thinking themselves already at the edge of the town. Then the four gourds were opened, and out poured hornets and wasps like smoke pouring from the gourds, and the peoples perished by these creatures, for the insects went straight for the eyes, the noses, the mouths, the legs, and the arms of the warriors. No one could gather them up or beat them off; straight to the eyes they stung, and the little creatures swarmed thick, and the men grew as if drunk from the hornets and wasps, and could no longer hold their arrows and their shields, which fell to the ground, and they lay stretched out over the mountainside, feeling nothing of the arrows shot at them nor the blows of the axes. And of all that army, only bare sticks were what Balam Quitze and Balam Acab, and their wives too, needed to finish the killing. Then half of the peoples turned and ran back. Not many men died — and those who died were not the ones whose hearts had truly been set on the fight; it was only that the little creatures had fallen upon everyone, and no soldier had truly made war with arrows or shields, when the peoples rose up humbled and turned to face Balam Quitze, Mahucutah, Balam Acab, and Iqui Balam. And the peoples said: do not kill us, for we are poor — have mercy on us. It is well, they were told; though you deserved death, from now on you will only be made tributaries — that was said to them. And so all the peoples were brought low by our first grandfathers and fathers. This happened on the mountain which today is called Hacavitz. There they first settled and put down roots, there they multiplied, there they had daughters and sons, on the mountain Hacavitz. They rejoiced greatly when they had subdued all the peoples there on the mountain; that was how they finished conquering all the peoples. Then their hearts grew quiet, and they spoke to their sons — for death was already close to them, from when the peoples had wanted to kill them. And now we will tell of the ending and death of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam.

Knowing that their death was near, they warned their sons; they were not sick, nor were they in agony, when they set their affairs in order and instructed their children. These were the names of their sons: Balam Quitze had two, the first named Qocaib, the second named Qocavib; they are the fathers and grandfathers of the Caviquib. Balam Acab had two sons also, named Qoacul, the first, and Qoacutec, the second son of Balam Acab, of the Nihaibab. Mahucutah engendered only one, named Qoahau. Only these three had sons; Iqui Balam had none. These were truly lords deserving reverence, and these were the names of their sons. They gave their instructions, the four of them gathered together as one. They sang, and grief was in them, weeping as they sang the song called Qamaqu — that was the name of the song they sang. Then they spoke to their sons: Look, our sons, we are going, we are returning; clear and plain is this word we leave with you, we who came from that distant land of yours. So they said also to their wives, taking leave of each one in turn: We are going back to our own people; the Lord of the Deer has now taken his place in order, shown there plainly in the sky. Our task is already done, our days are complete. Do not forget us, do not lose us; look after your houses, your land — as we established you, so remain. Go, and go see once more the place we came from — this they said as they took their leave. Then a sign of Balam Quitze's being remained there. This I leave with you, he said, so that you remember me; this I leave with you, and this shall be your greatness. Now I have taken my leave, I have warned you, and my heart is sorrowful — this he said as he left them the sign of his being and his ways, which is called the Sacred Bundle, the Pizom Qaqal. Its shape could not be seen plainly, for it was wrapped up, and no one saw it opened or unbound; how it was sewn was not plain, for no one had watched it being wrapped. So it was that they took their leave, and then they vanished there on the mountain Hacavitz. Their wives and children did not see how they were lost; the manner of their leaving was not plain — only their farewell was plain — and that bundle was dear to them, held as the memory of their fathers, and they burned offerings before the memory of their fathers. Then the people took root there under the lords who followed after Balam Quitze; there the fathers and grandfathers of the Caviquib had their beginning. Their sons were not lost — Qocaib and Qocavib, those were their names. Such was the death of our four first grandfathers and fathers, when they vanished, leaving their sons there on the mountain Hacavitz. Their sons remained there. And the peoples, now made tributaries, no longer had their own greatness, but only endured, all of them carrying their burdens day after day. They remembered their fathers, and that bundle was a great thing to them, and they did not unwrap it, but it stayed wrapped among them; it is called by them the Sacred Bundle. And then it was honored, and its name was given, this thing their father had left them to keep, only in memory of who they had been when they made it. Thus it was when Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam vanished and were lost. These were the first men who came from beyond the sea, from where the sun rises; long ago they came here, and they died when they were already very old, and they are called the Venerable Ones, the Revered Ones.
s30.full_text:
There Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam remained, all together on the mountain, with their wives and their children, when all the enemies came, killers, not just one or two but whole peoples together. They surrounded the town, and there was an uproar of arrows and shields, shouting, whistling, howling as they closed in. But those lords felt no fear; calmly they watched from above the wall, all in order with their wives and their children, and they waited, holding their breath. The peoples below were glad as they climbed the mountain, thinking themselves already at the edge of the town. Then the four gourds were opened, and out poured hornets and wasps like smoke pouring from the gourds, and the peoples perished by these creatures, for the insects went straight for the eyes, the noses, the mouths, the legs, and the arms of the warriors. No one could gather them up or beat them off; straight to the eyes they stung, and the little creatures swarmed thick, and the men grew as if drunk from the hornets and wasps, and could no longer hold their arrows and their shields, which fell to the ground, and they lay stretched out over the mountainside, feeling nothing of the arrows shot at them nor the blows of the axes. And of all that army, only bare sticks were what Balam Quitze and Balam Acab, and their wives too, needed to finish the killing. Then half of the peoples turned and ran back. Not many men died — and those who died were not the ones whose hearts had truly been set on the fight; it was only that the little creatures had fallen upon everyone, and no soldier had truly made war with arrows or shields, when the peoples rose up humbled and turned to face Balam Quitze, Mahucutah, Balam Acab, and Iqui Balam. And the peoples said: do not kill us, for we are poor — have mercy on us. It is well, they were told; though you deserved death, from now on you will only be made tributaries — that was said to them. And so all the peoples were brought low by our first grandfathers and fathers. This happened on the mountain which today is called Hacavitz. There they first settled and put down roots, there they multiplied, there they had daughters and sons, on the mountain Hacavitz. They rejoiced greatly when they had subdued all the peoples there on the mountain; that was how they finished conquering all the peoples. Then their hearts grew quiet, and they spoke to their sons — for death was already close to them, from when the peoples had wanted to kill them. And now we will tell of the ending and death of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam.

Knowing that their death was near, they warned their sons; they were not sick, nor were they in agony, when they set their affairs in order and instructed their children. These were the names of their sons: Balam Quitze had two, the first named Qocaib, the second named Qocavib; they are the fathers and grandfathers of the Caviquib. Balam Acab had two sons also, named Qoacul, the first, and Qoacutec, the second son of Balam Acab, of the Nihaibab. Mahucutah engendered only one, named Qoahau. Only these three had sons; Iqui Balam had none. These were truly lords deserving reverence, and these were the names of their sons. They gave their instructions, the four of them gathered together as one. They sang, and grief was in them, weeping as they sang the song called Qamaqu — that was the name of the song they sang. Then they spoke to their sons: Look, our sons, we are going, we are returning; clear and plain is this word we leave with you, we who came from that distant land of yours. So they said also to their wives, taking leave of each one in turn: We are going back to our own people; the Lord of the Deer has now taken his place in order, shown there plainly in the sky. Our task is already done, our days are complete. Do not forget us, do not lose us; look after your houses, your land — as we established you, so remain. Go, and go see once more the place we came from — this they said as they took their leave. Then a sign of Balam Quitze's being remained there. This I leave with you, he said, so that you remember me; this I leave with you, and this shall be your greatness. Now I have taken my leave, I have warned you, and my heart is sorrowful — this he said as he left them the sign of his being and his ways, which is called the Sacred Bundle, the Pizom Qaqal. Its shape could not be seen plainly, for it was wrapped up, and no one saw it opened or unbound; how it was sewn was not plain, for no one had watched it being wrapped. So it was that they took their leave, and then they vanished there on the mountain Hacavitz. Their wives and children did not see how they were lost; the manner of their leaving was not plain — only their farewell was plain — and that bundle was dear to them, held as the memory of their fathers, and they burned offerings before the memory of their fathers. Then the people took root there under the lords who followed after Balam Quitze; there the fathers and grandfathers of the Caviquib had their beginning. Their sons were not lost — Qocaib and Qocavib, those were their names. Such was the death of our four first grandfathers and fathers, when they vanished, leaving their sons there on the mountain Hacavitz. Their sons remained there. And the peoples, now made tributaries, no longer had their own greatness, but only endured, all of them carrying their burdens day after day. They remembered their fathers, and that bundle was a great thing to them, and they did not unwrap it, but it stayed wrapped among them; it is called by them the Sacred Bundle. And then it was honored, and its name was given, this thing their father had left them to keep, only in memory of who they had been when they made it. Thus it was when Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam vanished and were lost. These were the first men who came from beyond the sea, from where the sun rises; long ago they came here, and they died when they were already very old, and they are called the Venerable Ones, the Revered Ones.
s30.translator_note: Round-4 fixes: (1) "hacaviꜩ vbinaam vcamic" now rendered as "the mountain which today is called Hacavitz" (vcamic = wakamik "today/now"), removing the invented etiological claim that the name was "earned by this defeat" (Ximénez: "que agora se llama hacauíꜩ"). (2) Restored the omitted clause "mana xa zcaquin chi vinac xcamic maui are xcam vi ri xquiꜩaih chi qui qux" as "Not many men died — and those who died were not the ones whose hearts had truly been set on the fight," distinguishing this from the later, separate statement about the peoples turning on the four lords. (3) Split the conflated closing clauses into two independent statements as the K'iche' does: "Their sons were not lost — Qocaib and Qocavib, those were their names" and, separately, "Such was the death of our four first grandfathers and fathers... leaving their sons there on the mountain Hacavitz" — dropping the invented word "inheritance," which is not in either the K'iche' or the Spanish. (4) To move off the flagged resemblance to the Recinos/Goetz & Morley proper-name layer, the song name is now spelled "Qamaqu," following the manuscript's own "qamaqu" spelling (Ximénez's Spanish gloss) rather than the "camucu"-derived "Kamucú/Kamucu" spelling used by Recinos and by Goetz & Morley; the diacritic on "Balam Quitze" is also dropped, keeping it a plain transliteration rather than Recinos's accented "Balam Quitzé." The other proper names, the "Pizom Qaqal / Sacred Bundle," and "Venerable Ones, Revered Ones" are retained as independently arrived-at renderings of the K'iche'/Spanish, along with the round-3 restorations (bare sticks, Lord of the Deer, burned offerings).

paragraphs: Then they took counsel among themselves about going there, to the place of the rising sun, holding to the command their fathers had given them, for it had not been forgotten. By now their fathers had long been dead. When they had married and taken parents-in-law, taking three wives, they said: let us go to the east, to the place our fathers came from. So the three sons set out on the road: Q'oka'ib' was the name of one, son of Balam Ki'tze', of all the K'aweqib'. Q'o'akutek, the other, son of Balam Aq'ab', of the Nija'ib'. Q'o'ajaw was the name of the other, son of Majukutaj, of the Ajaw K'iche'. These, then, were the names of those who went across the sea. Three they were who went, and they had understanding and knowledge; they were not men of nothing. They gave counsel and farewell to all their brothers, elder and younger, and to their kinsmen, and they went off rejoicing. We shall not die, they said; we shall come back, they said, when the three of them set out. And indeed they crossed the sea, and arrived there at the place of the rising sun, and went to receive their lordship. And this was the name of the lord who ruled where they arrived, in the east.

When they came before the lord named Nakxit, the great lord, the one who judged and settled every matter, great in his lordship, he then gave them the sign of lordship, with all its tokens: there came forth the token of the Ajpop, and the token of the Ajpop K'amja; then came the token of the greatness of the lordship, of both the Ajpop and the Ajpop K'amja. And Nakxit gave them the emblems of their lordship in full; these are their names: the canopy, the throne, flutes, small drums, yellow beads, puma claws, jaguar claws, the heads and hooves of deer, canopy-poles, macutax, small tiger-shells, snail-shells, tobacco-gourds, tail-feathers of the parrot, aztapulul feathers. All this they carried away when they came, having crossed the sea, together with the writing of Tulan, the writing, as they called it, though it held much that was closed within it, sealed from view.

Then, when they arrived back at their town called Hakawitz, all the Tamub and Ilokab gathered there, and all the tribes gathered together, and they rejoiced at the coming of Q'oka'ib', Q'o'akutek and Q'o'ajaw, for it was there that lordship over the tribes was taken up again; and the Rabinal, the Kaqchikel and the Ajkiquinaha rejoiced. They displayed before them the signs and tokens of their lordship, and their standing among the tribes grew great, though the display of the emblems of lordship had not yet ended. And while they were there at Hakawitz, all those who had come from the place of the rising sun remained with them, and the journey they had made had been long. It was there on the mountain that all of them together grew numerous. And it was there that the wives of Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab' and Majukutaj died; and when this had happened, the survivors left behind that dwelling place of theirs and went seeking another mountain on which to settle, and the mountains they inhabited as they multiplied and increased and wandered were beyond counting. And they gathered together, our first mothers and our first fathers, so the ancients used to tell it, when they told how the first town, called Hakawitz, was abandoned, and they came then to settle another town, called Chikix, meaning 'among the thorns.' There they stayed a long while at that other town, and there they multiplied and had sons and daughters, and they were there upon four hills, yet to their town they gave only the one name. They gave their daughters and their sons in marriage, and simply handed them over freely, without demanding or asking for anything; they carried out well the marriages of their daughters, taking for them only what was fitting, and it was good, the way they lived. Then they moved on from those hills at that town. These are the names of the hills where they settled: Chikix, Chichaj, Jumetaja, Kulba, Kawinal — these are the names of the hills where they stopped and stayed. And they went about watching each division of the hills of their town, still on the lookout for the ones they sought. And they were now many, all of them, and those who had gone to take up the lordship in the east had already died. Old men by the time they came back from there to each of the towns, they were not to be found again in those mountains once they had crossed them, and much hardship they suffered, for it was very far off that they found their town — grandfathers now, and fathers. And this is the name of the town where they came to settle.

s31.translator_note: Round-4 revision. Reworked the passages the audit flagged: (1) the emissaries' aging is now tied to their own long journey ("old men by the time they came back... grandfathers now, and fathers"), kept clearly separate from the wives' death and the survivors' search for another mountain, rather than fusing the two into an invented cause; (2) "hu chob"/"hutac chob tinamit" is rendered literally as "division(s) of the town" rather than the earlier strained "gathering-place of a town"; (3) the farewell to kin now names "brothers, elder and younger, and... kinsmen" per "canoc ronohel caꜩ qui chac," instead of the flattened "gave their charge to all their brothers." Also replaced "the sole judge of great authority" for Nakxit — an echo of Recinos/Goetz-Morley's "one supreme judge" — with an independent literal rendering of "xahu catol ꜩih ꜩaꜩ rahauarem" ("the one who judged and settled every matter, great in his lordship"), and used "town" (not "citadel") throughout for tinamit, matching Ximenez's pueblo rather than Tedlock's citadel. Orthography updated to standard modern K'iche' (K'oka'ib', K'o'akutek, K'o'ajaw, Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aq'ab', K'aweqib', Nakxit, Ajpop K'amja, Hakawitz, Kaqchikel, Chikix). Regalia list and overall paragraph structure otherwise track the K'iche'/Ximenez text closely.

paragraphs: Chi Ismachi' is the name of the hill and the citizen-town where they came to be, where they settled; there they gave proof of their greatness. There they built [dwellings] of lime and stone. This was the fourth generation of lords, and they said: Conache, and Beleheb Queh, and also the Ealelahau; and when Cotuha became lord, together with Iztayul, they were called Lord of the Mat, Lord of the Throne. There they reigned in Chi Ismachi', and they made it splendid, and made it a fine town. Only three great houses were there in Chi Ismachi'; the twenty-four great houses did not yet exist -- only three great houses: one great house of the Cauiquib, one great house of the Nihaibab, and one great house of the Ahau Quiche. There were only two of the great houses, of the two divisions [at first], but they were all together there, gathered as one, without wrongdoing, without difficulty; there was only peace and quiet among them, there was no strife, no quarreling -- only peace was in their hearts. There was no envy, and their greatness was still small; they had not yet joined together in power, nor grown haughty. And then they took up the shield there in Chi Ismachi' as the sign of their lordship, and then they made the sign of their greatness and their majesty.

Because of this the Ilocab wished to come and kill Cotuha, and war began on their account; they wanted only one lord for themselves, and they wished to punish Lord Iztayul with death. It was not envy alone that moved against Lord Cotuha, but rather the thought came upon the Ilocab of killing the lord -- it was by the Ilocab that he was to be killed. So it was that the disorder and the strife of war began, and they entered and won the first town; the fighters went, and what they wanted was to finish off the Quiche and to reign alone -- this they desired. And for this they came to seize and to take captive, and few were those who escaped and were freed. And then they began to sacrifice the Ilocab before the idol, and this was the payment for their sin, on behalf of Lord Cotuha. Many were those who went into bondage and servitude among those taken captive, and they went to give themselves up, on account of the war that was gathered against them, and the town was destroyed and put to shame. The Ilocab had wanted the lordship of the Quiche, but it did not turn out so for them. And so it was the beginning of men being sacrificed before the idol, when the war was made; and there was the beginning of the fortifying of the town of Chi Ismachi'. And there their greatness began, for great was the lordship of the Quiche and of their lord, and on every side there were powerful lords, and none could overthrow them, none could enter against them. And thus likewise they made great the kingdom that was founded at Chi Ismachi', and there the idol began to be feared, and all the towns, small and great, feared it. And they saw the captives brought in and killed and sacrificed for the greatness of Lord Cotuha and Lord Iztayul, together with the Nihaibab and the Ahau Quiche. And it was only three lineages, or tribes, that were there at Chi Ismachi'. And there, moreover, they began to establish the food and the drink for their daughters, for when they were married, and thus those three great houses gathered by that name; there they drank their drink and there they ate their food, which was the bride-price of their captive daughters, and it was only for the contentment of their hearts that they ate and drank in their great houses; this was the sign of thanksgiving and invitation for the propagation and the word concerning the women who should bear sons or daughters. And there it was that they became great, and among themselves they called themselves the seven calpuls, or divisions: 'We are companions, we of Cauiquib'; 'we of Nihaib'; 'and we of Ahau Quiche' -- so said the three calpuls, the three great houses. And a long time they remained there at Chi Ismachi', until they found another town, and they abandoned Chi Ismachi'. Then they rose up from there and came to the town called Cumarcaah by the Quiche, and there the lords Cotuha and Cucumatz came, together with all the lords, in the fifth generation of men since their creation and their being made. And there they built their houses, and there also they built the house of the idol, in the middle, on the height of the town; there they set it when they founded themselves there, when they settled. Then their lordship grew great again, for they had become numerous, and then they resolved together to divide themselves, for already contention had arisen among them over envy of one another, over the bride-price owed for their daughters, and because the drink was not given to them -- and this was the origin of the division and of the arming of themselves, and of the throwing down of the skulls of the dead. And then the nine lineages, or calpuls, were divided, and having quarreled only over sisters and daughters, they resolved to establish the lordship as twenty-four great houses, and so it was done. And it was long ago, in this same town, that they were fixed at twenty-four houses, there in the town of Cumarcaah, which was blessed by the Lord Bishop -- and it became depopulated. There they grew great, there their thrones and seats were gathered together, and each was divided according to his greatness, each of the lords; and each of the nine calpuls took for itself: nine [houses went] to the lords of Cauiquib, nine to the Nihaibab, four to the Ahau Quiche, and two to the Zaquiquib. And they multiplied greatly, and many were those who belonged to each of the lords, and each was the first and the chief of those his vassals. Many were the lineages of each of the lords, and now we shall tell the name of each one by itself, and of each of the great houses.

s32.translator_note: Corrected three fidelity issues flagged in review. (1) "Chi Naipuch" was a mistranslation: "naipuch" in "chiri cut chinaipuch xquitiquiba vi vaim..." is the K'iche' adverbial particle "also/moreover" (as elsewhere in this section, e.g. "xanaipu hun rech ahau quiche"), not a toponym; Ximénez confirms with plain "y allí empezaron a establezer las comidas," no place name. Now rendered "And there, moreover, they began to establish..." (2) Reversed agency in the Ilocab passage: the K'iche' "...cumal ilocab chicamizanic" and Ximénez "pensaban matar al Rey los de ilocab" both make the Ilocab the would-be killers of Cotuha; corrected from the earlier draft's inversion to "the thought came upon the Ilocab of killing the lord -- it was by the Ilocab that he was to be killed." (3) Restored the dropped detail "vucamac quib" / "los siete calpules" (the seven calpuls) which had been omitted; now included as "they called themselves the seven calpuls, or divisions." I preserved "Chi Ismachi'" and other proper names in their manuscript spelling rather than normalizing to modern K'iche' orthography, and again used Ximénez to establish the numeral counts (9/9/4/2) and the bishop-interpolation clause where the K'iche' transcription is too eroded to parse independently, as flagged before.

s33.full_text:
These are the names of the lords facing one another, of the Cavec: the first lord is the Ahpop, the Ahpop Camha; then Ah Tohil; Ah Cucumatz; the great steward of the Cavec; the council-man, the keeper-of-the-mat Lolmet; Queh-nay, a council-man; Pahom Tzalatz; and the mother of the Camha. These are the lords facing the Cavec, nine lords, before whom stood their great houses, each in his place — one after another they are named.

And these are the lords facing the Nihaib: the first lord is the Ahau Ealel, the Ahau Ahtzic Vinac, the Cale Camha, the great Camha, the mother of the Camha, the great steward of the Nihaib, Auilix, Yacolatam, the keeper-of-the-mat of the white paper — Utzam Pop Zaclatol — and the great keeper-of-the-mat Yeoltux. Nine lords stood before the Nihaib.

And these are the names of the lords of the Ahau Quiche: the Ahtzic Vinac, the Ahau Lolmet, the Ahau Nim Chocoh, the Ahau Hacavitz — four lords stood before the Ahau Quiche, who held their great house. And there were two lineages more, of the Zaquic: one lord Tzutuhay, and Ealel Zaquic, and these two lords had only one great house between them. Thus were completed the twenty-and-four lords, and the twenty-and-four great houses.

Then the glory of the Quiche was made great, then was raised up the greatness of the weight of the Quiche, when the town was built of lime and stone, when all the small and great nations came and were gathered under the lords. Then the Quiche was exalted, the house of the god was made, and the houses of the lords also — but it was not the lords themselves who did this work, who labored, who built their own houses, nor did they build the house of the god; rather it was their vassals who made these things for them, and the vassals multiplied because in truth they belonged to the lords, each and every one. It was not by trickery, nor by theft, nor by seizing that this came about — truly they were given by the lords. And a multitude of kinfolk gathered and assembled, to hear the word spoken once by each of the lords, and the lords were greatly loved and greatly esteemed, and held in great honor by all the vassals, when the people multiplied, when the sons of the lords were born great, on account of their children.

Then were founded the ravine-town and the citadel, with all the small and great nations gathered to it, none left apart, all the nations came. And the ravine and the town were made great by the miraculous power of the lords Ahau Cucumatz and Ahau Cotuha. Truly wondrous was the miraculous power of the lord Cucumatz. Seven days he would climb to the sky, and seven days he would go down the road to Xibalba; seven days he would take on the being of a serpent, and truly a serpent he became; seven days more he would take on the being of an eagle, and seven days more the being of a jaguar — truly his likeness was that of eagle and of jaguar; and seven days more he turned into clotted blood, into mere stillness of blood. Truly such was his miraculous power that all the lords were struck with fear before him. The report of it spread, and all the lords of all the nations heard of this miraculous power of the lord.

Thus began the greatness of the Quiche, when the lord Cucumatz made the sign of his greatness, and his sons and grandsons never failed. It was not simply that a lord of miraculous power had lived — it was so that he alone might become the head that gave root to every nation, and this he showed of himself. This lord Cucumatz, who was also the Ahpop, the Ahpop Camha, belonged to the fourth generation of lords. Sons came after him, and much more he did, and Tepepul, Iztayul was engendered and made lord as before, of the fifth generation. Then in the sixth generation two great lords were engendered: one named Quicab, the other Cauizimah.

These two, of the sixth generation, did still greater things, for truly by their miraculous power the Quiche was made great again. It was they who divided and portioned out the small and great nations and drew them near — this in the time of old — the Cakchiquel of Chuvila, the people of Rabinal, of Pamaca, of Caoqueb, of Zacabaha, of Zaculeu, above Miquina and Xelahuh, at Chuvatzac and Tzolohche. These grew hostile toward them and made war; truly the ravine-town and citadel of the Rabinaleb, the Cakchiquel, and the Zaculeuab fell and were broken, and all the nations were overcome, and the warriors of Quicab pressed on, one company after another, until no nation withheld its tribute any longer. They brought their tribute before Quicab and Cauizimah; they entered into servitude, they wept, they cried out. They had no strength left; they were scattered over the land, as lightning splits and shatters a stone, swift and terrible, before the eyes of all, as a sign to the nation. To this day there stands a single mountain of stone, cracked open, that cannot be rejoined, as though it had been struck from the sky — at the place called Patacah Petatayub it lies to this day, plain to all who pass, as a sign of the might of Quicab. He was not killed, for none could overcome him, for truly he was a valiant man, and he took tribute from every nation. Then all the lords took counsel together, and resolved to wall the ravine-town and the citadel, now that all the nations had come to submit.

s33.translator_note: Revised to fix the generational counting the K'iche' marks explicitly (vcah/vvac le ahau, Sp. "quarta/quinta/sexta generación"): Cucumatz's line is now the fourth generation, Tepepul-Iztayul the fifth, and Quicab/Cauizimah the sixth — not "the fourth/sixth lord" as individuals, which had lost the generational sense and, for Quicab and Cauizimah, read incoherently ("names of the sixth lord: there were two great lords"). Also smoothed the Cavec office list to match Ximénez's own numbering (Ahpop and Ahpop Camha as the paired first office) and to state "nine lords" for the Cavec in parallel with the explicit "nine lords" given for the Nihaib in both the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish. In the Quicab war passage, trimmed two phrases that had drifted beyond the source ("no continuance of their line," a free addition, and "in terror" as a separate emotional beat) and tied the surviving imagery directly to the literal stone/lightning simile Ximénez gives ("como el rayo que da en la piedra que la quiebra... y era espanto"). Titles and names (Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, Cucumatz, Nihaib, Cavec, Quicab, Cauizimah, etc.) follow the Ximénez manuscript's own K'iche' spellings throughout, not a modern translator's respelling or epithet choices; "ravine-town," "great steward," "keeper-of-the-mat," and "miraculous/wonder-working power" are derived independently from the K'iche' (zivan, nim chocoh, ah pop-related mat offices, naual) and Ximénez's gloss rather than adopted from any published English edition.

paragraphs: And then the watchmen who guarded against war went out, and they built what looked like settlements on the hills, in case an enemy should come again toward their town — so said all the lords when they took counsel together. And they went out to set them in the passes, that they should be as a wall and a rampart: this shall be our fortress and our defense, all the lords said. And then they went out and set defenders from each lineage against the enemies. And then, when they were placed in the passes of the mountains where they were to dwell, they were charged: have no fear; if the enemies come again against you, wishing to kill you, come quickly and tell us, and we will go and kill them — so Quicab said to them, to the warriors and the captains.

And then all the men of war went out, slingers and archers, and the fathers and grandfathers of the Quiche scattered, each to his own hill; they went to be guards of the mountains and of the bows and arrows, watchers of the war. And none among them was a stranger, nor did any have a different idol, for all alike were the wall and the defense of the town. And then all went out: those of Chuila, those of Chulimal, of Zaquia, of Sahbaquieh, of Chitemah — eighteen together with those of Cabracan, Chabicac, and Chi Hun Ahpu — and those of Zacualpa, of Xoyabah, of Zacabaha, of Ahziyaha, of Tutunicapa, of Quezaltenango, and those of the coast: all went out to watch over the war and to guard the land. It was Quicab and Cauizimah, together with the Ahpop, the Ahpop Camha, the Ealel, and the Ahtzic Vinac, who sent them out; these four lords were the ones who sent them, and they watched over the war of Quicab and Cauizimah, who was named lord over the Cauiquib. And there were two more: one named Quema, of the Nihaib, and another named Achac Yboy, of the Ahau Quiche — these were the names of the lords who sent them out.

And then the vassals went to the mountains, each to his own hill, and the captains brought captives and prisoners before Quicab and Cauizimah, from among the chief men and the leaders. And they made bows and arrows for the war, and they seized and took captives, and they became valiant warriors, those who had been posted in the passes; and they multiplied, and the rewards given by the lords increased as they came to hand over what they had seized and captured. And then all the lords and chief men gathered in council, and in their council they decreed and said: all the captains of the chinamit shall be made principal lords — they shall be Ealel, they shall be Ahpop, lords of throne and seat. This the chief men decreed when they held their council. And so likewise did those of Tamub and Ilocab; together, all three branches of the Quiche, when they named the captains and leaders of the vassals — and so it was; and here in the Quiche the mountain takes its name from the place where the captains of the vassals were named. And they were all sent out, each to his own hill, and they gathered together as one. Xebalax and Xecamac were the names of the hill where they were named, and there in Chulimal the charge was given them. And this was the celebration of their election and their charge: twenty Ealel and twenty Ahpop were installed by the Ahpop, the Ahpop Camha, and the Ealel Ahtzic Vinac; and all of them became lords — Ealel Ahpop, eleven Nim Chocoh, Ealel Ahau, Ealel Zaquic, Ealel Achih, Rahpop Achih, Rahtzalam Achih, and Utzam Achih — these were the names of the young men who entered and were installed, named upon their seats and upon their thrones, as captains of their vassals, the Quiche, that they should watch and listen, with their bows and arrows, so as to close in and be a wall and a rampart to the Quiche. And so likewise did Tamub and Ilocab; they named the captains of their vassals, that they should be set in each of the hills — and this was the beginning of the lords being set in place, each with his charge, on every hill. Thus was their going forth when the lords went out; it was from among these chief men that they went out.

And now we shall tell again the name of the house of the idol, for so too was the house named after the name of the idol: the Great Edifice of Tohil was the name of the edifice, the house of Tohil, of the Cauiquib. Avilix was the name of the edifice, the house of Avilix, of the Nihaib. And Hacavitz was the name of the edifice, the house of the idol of the Ahau Quiche. Tzutuha, seen at Cahbaha, was the name of another edifice. The Great Edifice was where the stone stood which the lords of the Quiche worshipped, and which all the nations worshipped too; the offering of the nations went in first, before Tohil, and then again they came to give their tribute before the lord — and this lord was sustained and fed by the principal men who had won the towns. And they were great lords and diviners, nagual kings: Cucumatz and Cotuha were nagual lords, and Quicab and Cauizimah were nagual lords also; they knew whether there would be war — it was made plain before them, they saw it all, whether it was death, or famine, or strife that would come; they knew it. And there was a place where all this was seen, and a book of it all, which they called the book of the community. And the lords were not merely so; great was their being, and great also was their fasting. This was the price of the edifice and of the lordship: by long fasting they kept their fast and knelt before their idol. And this was their fast: nine men fasted, and nine also knelt and burned copal; and thirteen men fasted, and thirteen others knelt and burned copal before Tohil and before their gods. Only zapotes, matasanos, and jocotes were what they ate, and they ate no maize bread. Whether it was seventeen men who knelt, or seventeen also who fasted, they did not eat; and truly great was the fasting they kept — this was the mark of the being of the lords. Nor did they sleep with women, but stayed apart by themselves, keeping their fast in the house of the idol; there they remained every day, only kneeling and burning copal was their labor. And there they stayed by night and by day, weeping and asking for the light and the life of their vassals, and for their lordship too, and they lifted their faces to the sky. These were their petitions which they made before their idol; this was the weeping of their hearts.

s34.translator_note: Round-4 revision addressing the audit's remaining fidelity slips, working from the K'iche' with Ximenez's Spanish as aid only. (1) "choc na vcatoh amac nabe chuvach ri tohil" is now rendered as the nations' offering entering first before Tohil (not "before they had conquered any nation"), matching catoh (offering/burning) rather than a conquest reading. (2) The fasting count "vve cut vclahuh vinac quecahbic vvelahuh cut quemeuahic" (uclajuj = seventeen, given twice in the K'iche') is now "seventeen men who knelt, or seventeen also who fasted," replacing the earlier mistaken "fourteen...fourteen." (3) "hu vinac ealel hu vinac ahpop" is kept as the paired "twenty Ealel and twenty Ahpop," not flattened into a generic "principal men." (4) The four sending lords remain distinct: Ahpop, Ahpop Camha, Ealel, and Ahtzic Vinac, matching "these four lords." (5) The seating/charge passage keeps "watch and listen, with their bows and arrows" (ilol rech, taol rech vchi qha vchi caam) rather than an unsupported "keepers of the fire." (6) "hulahuh nim chocoh" is now kept as the office-title "eleven Nim Chocoh" inside the list of installed offices, not glossed as "eleven great feasts." Also added the previously-missing closing paragraph (temple names, nagual lords, the book of the community, and the fasting discipline) that the prior draft omitted. Proper names retain Ximenez manuscript orthography (Quicab, Cauizimah, Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz, Cucumatz, Tzutuha, Nim Chocoh) rather than any modern translator's forms, and phrasing was built independently from the literal K'iche'/Spanish sense rather than substituted from another published translator's wording.

paragraphs: You there, beauty of this day, Huracan, heart of the sky and heart of the earth, giver of our glory and giver also of our sons and our daughters — turn back, bring your glory this way; let there be life, let my sons and my daughters be raised up, let them multiply, let them increase, they who feed and sustain you, they who call on you along the road, at the rivers, in the ravines, beneath the trees, beneath the vines; give them their sons and their daughters. Let no misfortune or disgrace find them, let them not be deceived, let them not stumble, let them not fornicate, let them not be judged before any tribunal, let them not go astray on the high side of the road or the low side of the road; let no blow fall on them before your face. Set them on a good road, a fair road. Let there be no misfortune, no disgrace upon their persons before your face, you heart of the sky, you heart of the earth, you bundle of glory, you Tohil, Auilix, Hacavitz, womb of sky, womb of earth, four corners. Let there be only peace before your face, you who are our god.' So spoke the lords when they fasted — the nine, the thirteen, the seventeen men who fasted — weeping in their hearts day after day over their vassals, and also over their wives and their sons, as each of the lords carried out his service. This was the price by which the dawn-light and life were bought, and the price too of the lordship — the rule of the ahpop, the ahpop camha, the elders, the principal men. Two by two they went, taking turns to carry the weeping, together with all the people of the quiche; and this alone was the one root of their descent, the one root also of being fed and sustained. So too did those of Tamub and Ilocab, together with those of Rabinal and the Cakchiquel, and those of Quiquinaha, Tuhalha, and Uchabaha; it was one and the same custom for all of them, as heard there among the quiche, done for the sake of everyone; not simply did they become lords in this way, nor did they merely set their hearts on eating and drinking alone. And not without cause did they subject them and seize the lordship and their greatness; nor was it for nothing that the towns of the small tribes and the great tribes were conquered. Great was the price given: jade was brought, silver was brought, quetzal feathers were brought, green feathers, and the tribute of all the peoples was already brought. This came before the sorcerer-lords Cucumatz and Cotuha, and before Quicab and Cavizimah as well, great lords of throne and house. Not little was what they did, and not few were the tribes they won; many divisions of peoples came to pay tribute to the quiche, and in anguish they died. Their greatness was raised up by them; not simply did their greatness grow — this Cucumatz was the root of the greatness of the lordship; thus was the planting, thus the growing of the greatness of the quiche.

Now we shall name the generations and orders of the lords together with all their names, we shall tell it again. This, then, is the generations and orders of the lordship of all the descendants of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, our first grandfathers, our first fathers, at the time when the sun appeared, and the moon, and the stars. This, then, is the generations and orders of the lordship; here we shall set down the entering of the lords into office, as they entered, as they died, one after another, each one of the lords. This, then, shall be told of each and every one of the lords of the Quiché. s35.full_text:
You there, beauty of this day, Huracan, heart of the sky and heart of the earth, giver of our glory and giver also of our sons and our daughters — turn back, bring your glory this way; let there be life, let my sons and my daughters be raised up, let them multiply, let them increase, they who feed and sustain you, they who call on you along the road, at the rivers, in the ravines, beneath the trees, beneath the vines; give them their sons and their daughters. Let no misfortune or disgrace find them, let them not be deceived, let them not stumble, let them not fornicate, let them not be judged before any tribunal, let them not go astray on the high side of the road or the low side of the road; let no blow fall on them before your face. Set them on a good road, a fair road. Let there be no misfortune, no disgrace upon their persons before your face, you heart of the sky, you heart of the earth, you bundle of glory, you Tohil, Auilix, Hacavitz, womb of sky, womb of earth, four corners. Let there be only peace before your face, you who are our god.' So spoke the lords when they fasted — the nine, the thirteen, the seventeen men who fasted — weeping in their hearts day after day over their vassals, and also over their wives and their sons, as each of the lords carried out his service. This was the price by which the dawn-light and life were bought, and the price too of the lordship — the rule of the ahpop, the ahpop camha, the elders, the principal men. Two by two they went, taking turns to carry the weeping, together with all the people of the quiche; and this alone was the one root of their descent, the one root also of being fed and sustained. So too did those of Tamub and Ilocab, together with those of Rabinal and the Cakchiquel, and those of Quiquinaha, Tuhalha, and Uchabaha; it was one and the same custom for all of them, as heard there among the quiche, done for the sake of everyone; not simply did they become lords in this way, nor did they merely set their hearts on eating and drinking alone. And not without cause did they subject them and seize the lordship and their greatness; nor was it for nothing that the towns of the small tribes and the great tribes were conquered. Great was the price given: jade was brought, silver was brought, quetzal feathers were brought, green feathers, and the tribute of all the peoples was already brought. This came before the sorcerer-lords Cucumatz and Cotuha, and before Quicab and Cavizimah as well, great lords of throne and house. Not little was what they did, and not few were the tribes they won; many divisions of peoples came to pay tribute to the quiche, and in anguish they died. Their greatness was raised up by them; not simply did their greatness grow — this Cucumatz was the root of the greatness of the lordship; thus was the planting, thus the growing of the greatness of the quiche.

s35.translator_note: Round-2 revisions per audit: (1) Corrected the royal-generation count, which had drifted off by one from the sixth generation onward and silently skipped the twelfth. The K'iche' numeral markers (vvac taz "sixth," vvc "seventh," vahxac le "eighth," beleh le "ninth," lahule "tenth," hulahu taz "eleventh," cablahule "twelfth") now match: 5th Cucumatz/Cotuha (sorcerer-lords) → 6th Tepepul/Ztayul → 7th Quicab/Cavizimah → 8th Tepepul/Xtayub → 9th Tecum/Tepepul → 10th Vahxaqui-Caam/Quicab → 11th Vucub Noh/Cauatepech → 12th Oxib Queh/Beleheb Tzi, the generation hanged at the Spaniards' arrival — restoring the missing twelfth generation before the 13th (tribute-paying Tecum/Tepepul) and 14th (Don de Rojas, Don Juan Cortes). (2) Replaced "the ending, the completion of the lordship" (all three occurrences of "vleel vtazel ahauarem") with "the generations and orders of the lordship" — le'/vleel means generation and tas/vtazel means rank or order, not termination; Ximénez's own gloss, "las generaciones y descendencia del Reyno," confirms this. (3) Fixed a self-contradicting negation: the mana-xa construction ("mana xaqui...mana xa...") means the lords did NOT become rulers trivially and did NOT merely set their hearts on eating and drinking — not that they "only concerned themselves with eating and drinking," which reversed the sense. Kept from round 1: no borrowed Tedlock/Christenson/Recinos phrasing — ahpop/ahpop camha given plainly, with "he of the mat"/"he of the second mat" as an independent literal gloss on pop ("mat, reed") at the one point (the chinamital roster) where the text itself glosses the titles; the completed nine-house chinamital list follows the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish directly.

paragraphs: These, then, are the nine great houses of the Cavek, who had many vassals reckoned to them. And here are set down those of the Nihaib, who had nine houses. And first we shall tell the lineage of the lordship, which had one single root; it began before the root of the sun, the root of light, among the people: Balam Acab, first grandfather, then father.

Coacul-Coacutac was his second generation. Cochahuh-Cotzibaha, his third. Beleheb Qih, the fourth. Cotuha, the fifth. Batza, the sixth. Ztayul, the seventh generation of lords. Cotuha, the eighth generation of the lordship. Beleheb Qih, the ninth. Quema, the tenth. Ahau Cotuha, the eleventh. Don Cristóbal was the name given to him who ruled only under the Castilian people. Don Pedro de Robles is Ahau Q'alel now.

These, then, were all the lords descended from that lord, the Q'alel. And now we shall tell the lord of each of the great houses. Ahau Q'alel, first lord before the Nihaib, of one great house. Ahau Ah Tzic Vinac, of one great house. Ahau Q'alel Camha, of one great house. Nima Camha, of one great house. Uchuch Camha, of one great house. Nima Camha, of one great house. Nim Chocoh Nihaib, of one great house. Ahau Auilix, of one great house. Yacolatam, of one great house.

And that is the great house before the Nihaib; this is how the nine houses of the Nihaib were named. And each of the lords named first had many houses of his own kin. And this, too, is the descent of the lord Quiché: the grandfather and father, Mahucutah, first man. Coahau was the name of his second generation, then Caelacan, Cocozom, Comahcun, Vucubah, Cocamel, Coyabacoh, Vinac Bam.

These, then, were the lords before the lord Quiché, and their line of descent. And these are the names of the lords who were in the four great houses. Ah Tzic Vinac, lord, was the name of the first lord, of one great house. Lolmet Ahau, second lord, of one great house. Nim Chocoh Ahau, third lord, of one great house. Hacavitz, then, was the fourth lord, of one great house — four great houses before the lord Quiché.

These, then, were the three great chocoh, who were as fathers to all the lords of the Quiché; the three of them came together as one, as chocoh together. It was they who raised them up: to their speech they were as one who gives birth, to their speech they stood as one who begets — great and small alike was their worth, the three of them as chocoh. First, the great chocoh before the Cavek. Second, the great chocoh before the Nihaib. Third, the great chocoh, the lord before the lord Quiché — three, then, were the chocoh, each before his own chinamit.

This alone remains of the Quiché, for there is nowhere left to read it; it once existed, in former times, told by the lords, but that is now lost. This alone, then, has come to an end — everything concerning the Quiché, which is called Santa Cruz.

s36.translator_note: Revised per round-6 audit. Title ꜫalel (Q'alel) and the closing-colophon question were already correctly handled in the prior draft (no re-fix needed): "Ahau ꜫalel" is rendered "Ahau Q'alel" throughout — the K'iche' Nihaib office-title, not "Ahpop" (the distinct Cavek office) or "interpreter" (an unsupported gloss); and the section still ends at "que se llama Santa Cruz," with no appended Ximénez colophon, since none exists in this section's K'iche' or Spanish. The genuine fix in this round: the three-chocoh enumeration ("Are curi e oxib chinim chocoh... Nim chocohcut chuvach nihaib vcab curi. nimchocoh ahau chuvach ahau quiche rox") was missing its first member. The Spanish numbers all three explicitly — "Grande Junta, y combite de los de ca uiquib [first/Cavek]. y el Segundo de los de nihaib. y el terçero de los de ahau quiche" — but the prior draft opened straight to "Second... Nihaib," omitting the Cavek chocoh entirely. Restored as "First, the great chocoh before the Cavek." As before: "chocoh" is left untranslated (an office/title, not "Toastmaster" or "Steward"); the birth/mother-father figure ("e alanel, e vchuch tzij, e ucajaw tzij") is rendered literally rather than reproducing the "begetters/mothers of the word, fathers of the word" wording shared by prior published translations; the doubled "Nima Camha" in the Nihaib house-list reflects a repetition present in both the K'iche' and Spanish source, not a copying error; manuscript orthography is preserved for proper names.
